parole.significato: alternative form of -er (used chiefly after unstressed syllables, with occasional exceptions such as leraar, winnaar)
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz, which in Proto-Germanic times was borrowed from Latin -ārius. Doublet of -er and -der.

From Middle Dutch -achtig, partly from -haftig, which consists of -haft and -ig; and partly continuing Middle Dutch -echt, from Proto-Germanic *-ihtaz, *-ahtaz. The suffix -haft stems from Proto-Germanic *haftaz (“tied, captured”). Compare German -haft, -haftig and Danish -agtig.

parole.significato: -able, attaches to verbs to form an adjective that indicates that an action can be performed
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -baer, from Old Dutch *-bāri, from Proto-Germanic *bēriz, which belongs to the verb *beraną (“to bear”). See English bear (verb). Cognate with German -bar, Latin -fer.

parole.significato: indicates second person in inversion, substituting or supplementing gij; you
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -dī, from a contraction of the þ in Proto-Germanic *-aiþ (second person plural ending) and *jīz (“you (plural)”), somewhat comparable to Icelandic þér. Sometimes incorrectly seen as a remnant of Middle Dutch du (“you”).

parole.significato: Used to form abstract nouns from adjectives; the nouns express the quality of the adjective.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -e, from Old Dutch -i, from Proto-Germanic *-į̄.
From Middle Dutch -elen, from Old Dutch -lon, from Proto-Germanic *-lōną.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives that indicate the substance from which something is made.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -ijn, -in, -en, from Old Dutch *-īn, from Proto-Germanic *-īnaz.

parole.significato: Ending of the infinitive form of verbs.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -en, a merger of various Old Dutch infinitive suffixes: * The strong infinitive -an, from Proto-Germanic *-aną. * The weak class 1 infinitive -en, -ien, from Proto-Germanic *-janą, *-ijaną. * The weak class 2 infinitive -on, from Proto-Germanic *-ōną.

parole.significato: The ending of the past participle of strong verbs. This can also function as an adjective.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -en, from Old Dutch -an, from Proto-Germanic *-anaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-nós.
From Old Dutch *-āri, -ere, from Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz, borrowed from Latin -ārius. Cognate with Dutch -aar.

parole.significato: Forms nouns denoting male inhabitants or residents of a place.
parole.testo: From Old Dutch *-āri, -ere, from Proto-Germanic *warjaz.

parole.significato: Forms the comparative form of adjectives.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -er, from Old Dutch -iro, -oro, from Proto-Germanic *-izô, *-ōzô.

parole.significato: Forms nouns for the female counterpart of something.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -inne, from Old Dutch *-inna, from Proto-Germanic *-inī.

parole.significato: Used to form the genitive case of (strong) masculine and neuter nouns.
parole.testo: From the genitive case of masculine and neuter nouns and adjectives, Middle Dutch -s, -es, from Old Dutch -es, -is, from Proto-Germanic *-as, *-is.

parole.significato: appended to the stem of a verb, this suffix yields a verbal noun; it is similar in function to the Dutch suffix -ing
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *-þiz. The -s- is the result of a wrong segmentation of stem and suffix of a noun in cases where the stem of the noun ended with -s-. For example: a word like Dutch vorst (“frost”) could be interpreted as vors+t or as vor+st. This suffix existed already in Gothic (𐌰𐌽𐍃𐍄𐍃 (ansts),

parole.significato: appended to an adjective this suffix forms the superlative
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -st, from Old Dutch -ist, -ost, from Proto-Germanic *-istaz, *-ōstaz. Cognate of Afrikaans -ste, English -est, German -(e)st, Danish -(e)st, Swedish -(a)st.

parole.significato: -ty; used to form numerals denoting multiples of ten
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -tech, -tich, from Old Dutch *-tig, from Proto-Germanic *tigiwiz, plural of *teguz (“group of ten”). Cognate with German -zig and English -ty.

parole.significato: in or towards the direction referred to by the stem onto which this suffix has been appended; the resulting word is an…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -waerts < -weerts < -werts, from an adverbial genitive of Proto-Germanic *werdaz, byform of *wardaz (“turned to, facing”). Cognate with German -wärts, English -wards.

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives/adverbs of base adjective's quality; compare English -able, English -some
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -sam, later also -saem based on the inflected forms, from Old Dutch -sam, from Proto-Germanic *-samaz, from *samaz (“same”). Cognate with English -some, German -sam, Old Norse -samr.
From Middle Dutch â, from Old Dutch ā, from Proto-Germanic *ahwō.
From Middle Dutch âes, from Old Dutch ās, from Proto-Germanic *ēsaz.
From Middle Dutch achte, from Old Dutch *āhta, from Proto-Germanic *anhtō.

First attested in the 16th century, but probably a Middle Dutch formation based on achterdenken. The form -docht (from Proto-Germanic *þanhtaz) displays Ingvaeonic influence (compare Old English þōht, Old Frisian thōchte): achterdacht is the expected form, but is now long obsolete.
From Middle Dutch *achtetien, *achttien, from Old Dutch *ahtotēn, *ahtotien, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Compare West Frisian achttjin, German achtzehn, English eighteen, Danish atten.
From Middle Dutch af, from Old Dutch af, from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ab.

parole.significato: to hand off, hand over, deliver
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch avegeven, from Proto-Germanic *abagebaną; equivalent to af + geven.
From Middle Dutch afleggen, aveleggen, from Proto-Germanic *abalagjaną. Equivalent to af + leggen.
From Middle Dutch afnemen, avenemen, from Old Dutch avaneman, from Proto-Germanic *abanemaną; equivalent to af + nemen.
From Middle Dutch aker, from Old Dutch *akaran, from Proto-Germanic *akraną.
From Middle Dutch angel, from Old Dutch *angul, from Proto-Germanic *angulaz. Cognate with German Angel.

From Middle Dutch anxt, from Old Dutch *angust, from Proto-Germanic *angustiz, an abstract noun derived from the adjective *anguz. Similar abstract noun derivations from an adjective are dienst and ernst. Cognates include Middle Low German angest, Old High German angust, Middle High German angest, G
From Middle Dutch antworde, from Old Dutch andworde, from Proto-Germanic *andawurdiją. Cognate to German Antwort.
From Middle Dutch antworden, from Old Dutch antworden, from Proto-Germanic *andawurdijaną.
From Middle Dutch arre, erre, irre, from Old Dutch *irri, from Proto-Germanic *irzijaz.

parole.significato: to work, to do manual labour
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch arbeiden, from Old Dutch, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidijaną. Cognates include German arbeiten, Old Saxon arvedian, Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌱𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (arbaidjan). Equivalent to arbeid + -en.
From Middle Dutch asse, from Old Dutch *assa, from Proto-Germanic *ahsō.
From Middle Dutch bate, from Old Dutch *bato, from Proto-Germanic *batô.

parole.significato: The meat of a pig, pork.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *bak, bake, baec (“meat from the back of a pig”), from Old Dutch *bak (“back, rear”), from Proto-Germanic *baką. Cognate with English back, Icelandic bak. Etymologically related to bakboord and achterbaks.

parole.significato: baker (person who bakes and sells bread, etc)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch backer, from Old Dutch *bakar, *baker, from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz.
From Middle Dutch bernen, barnen, from Old Dutch *brinnan, from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną.

parole.significato: Used to indicate that a verb is acting on a direct object (making an intransitive verb into a transitive verb). Always…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch be-, bi-, from Old Dutch bi-, be-, from Proto-Germanic *bi-, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near, by”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“at, near”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian be- (“be-”), West Frisian be- (“be-”), English be-, German Low German be- (“be-”), German be- (

parole.significato: brook, creek (running waterway smaller than a river)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bēke, from Old Dutch beki, from Proto-Germanic *bakiz.

parole.significato: low-lying pasture or meadow near water, e.g. a floodplain or a grassy polder
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch beemt, bempt (13th century). Cognate with Limburgish baandj, Ripuarian Bänd (both roughly “hayfield, wet meadow, floodplain”). Thought to be derived from an underlying Middle Dutch *banmade (“communal hayfield”), from ban (“jurisdiction”) + made (“meadow”), respectively from Proto-
From Middle Dutch bēte, from Old Dutch *biti, from Proto-Germanic *bitiz.
From Middle Dutch begrāven, from Old Dutch bigravan, from Proto-Germanic *bigrabaną. Equivalent to be- + graven.
From Middle Dutch begroeten, from Old Dutch *bigruoten, from Proto-Germanic *bigrōtijaną. Equivalent to be- + groeten.
From Middle Dutch behagen, from Old Dutch *bihagon, from Proto-Germanic *bihagōną, from the root *hag-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱok- (“to be able”), see also Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬐- (sak-, “to agree”).

From Middle Dutch behoeven, from Old Dutch *bihuovon, from Proto-Germanic *bihōbōną. Equivalent to be- + hoeven. Cognate with English behove, behoove (“to be necessary for”), obsolete German behufen (cf. Behuf), Danish behøve (“to need”), Norwegian behøve (“to need”), Swedish behöva (“to have use fo
From Middle Dutch beiden, from Old Dutch beiden, from Proto-Germanic *baidijaną.
From Middle Dutch becōmen, from Old Dutch bikuman, from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną. Equivalent to be- + komen.
From Middle Dutch bequaem, from Proto-Germanic *bi-quēmi-, *bikwemaną. Doublet of bekomen. Cognate with German bequem.
From Middle Dutch belle, from Old Dutch bella, from Proto-Germanic *bellǭ.
From Middle Dutch belemmen, from Old Dutch *bilemmen, from Proto-Germanic *bilamjaną.
From Middle Dutch beneden, from Proto-Germanic *bi- + *niþanē (“from beneath”).
From Middle Dutch benēmen, from Old Dutch bineman, from Proto-Germanic *binemaną. Equivalent to be- + nemen.
From Middle Dutch bert (“plank, tabletop”), from Old Dutch *bret, from Proto-Germanic *bredą. Cognate with German Brett (“board, plank”).

parole.significato: to prepare (particularly of food and drink)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bereiden, from reiden, reden, from Old Dutch *reiden, from Proto-Germanic *raidijaną.

parole.significato: berm, verge, roadside (strip of land next to a road, street or sidewalk)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch baerm, from Old Dutch *barm, from Proto-Germanic *barmaz.

parole.significato: to rob [with van ‘of’], to steal from
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch berôven, from Old Dutch *birōvon, from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną; equivalent to be- + roven.
From Middle Dutch beschinen, from Old Dutch *biskīnan, from Proto-Germanic *biskīnaną. Equivalent to be- + schijnen. Cognate with English beshine.
From Middle Dutch beseffen, from Old Dutch *biseffen, from bi- + *seffen. The latter part is from Proto-Germanic *sabjaną.

From Middle Dutch smuyck, from Old Dutch smuyck. The prefix be- was added as phonetic contamination from the past participle of smuiken (“to be hidden or calm”). Compare also the related verbs smokkelen and smuiken, all ultimately from Proto-Germanic *smukkōną (“to slide, slip through”).
From Middle Dutch besprēken, from Old Dutch *bisprekan, from Proto-Germanic *bisprekaną. Equivalent to be- + spreken.
From Middle Dutch best, from Old Dutch *betst, from Proto-Germanic *batistaz, superlative of *gōdaz. Compare Low German best, English best, West Frisian best, German besten, Danish bedst.

parole.significato: to behoove, to be appropriate, fitting or necessary, to suit
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch betamen, from tamen (“to behove, befit”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tamōną, though exact cognates are lacking. Other Germanic languages have cognates with -e- or -i-: Old High German zeman (German ziemen), Old Saxon teman, Old Frisian timia, Old English temian (English beteem
From Middle Dutch bēteren, from Old Dutch *beteron, from Proto-Germanic *batizōną. Equivalent to beter + -en.
From Middle Dutch betogen, from togen, from Old Dutch tōgen, from Proto-Germanic *ataugijaną, a derivation of *augijaną, from *augô (“eye”) (modern oog).

parole.significato: to have a closer look at
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch besien, from Old Dutch bisian, from Proto-Germanic *bisehwaną (“to look, besee”), equivalent to be- + zien. Cognate with English besee, German besehen.
From Middle Dutch besitten, from Old Dutch besitten, from Proto-Germanic *bisitjaną (“to sit near, sit among”). Equivalent to be- + zitten.

parole.significato: buttock (each of the two large fleshy halves of the posterior part of the body between the base of the back, the perine…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bille, from a Proto-Germanic *balliją n, derived from *balluz (“ball”). Cognate with Old High German arsbelli, Middle High German arsbelle, Middle Low German bille (also with -e- in ārsbelle), modern Low German Bill(e), West Frisian bil. The last two mean mostly “fleshy part of the

parole.significato: a hammer-like double-edged tool used by stonecutters and millers
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bíþla- (“axe”), instrumental noun from *bītaną (“to bite”). However, compare *bilją (“blade, axe”), which could have influenced its development.

parole.significato: to sharpen, to apply grooves to a millstone
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch billen, probably ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bíþla- (“axe”), instrumental noun from *bītaną (“to bite”). Related to Old Norse bíldr (“bloodletting knife”).
From Middle Dutch blei, from Old Dutch *bleia. From Proto-Germanic *blaigijǭ (“blay, bleak, gudgeon”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyk- (“to shine”). Cognate with English blay.
From Middle Dutch blêken, from Old Dutch *blēken, from Proto-Germanic *blaikijaną. Equivalent to bleek (“pale”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch blenden, from Old Dutch *blenden, from Proto-Germanic *blandijaną.
From Middle Dutch blexeme, from Old Dutch blikisni (“lightning bolts”), ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivation of Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ-.
From Middle Dutch blinken, from Old Dutch *blinkan, from Proto-Germanic *blinkaną.

From Middle Dutch bloesem, bloeseme, (also bloesene), from Old Dutch *bluostmo, from Proto-Germanic *blōstmô. Compare Old English blostma ( > English blossom), Middle Low German blossem, blosem (“blossom”), Middle High German bluost (“blossom”). More at blossom.
From Middle Dutch blok, from Old Dutch *blok, from Proto-Germanic *blukką.

From Middle Dutch blosen, further etymology unclear, but ultimately from Proto-Germanic *blus-, perhaps related to *blasį̄ (“blaze”). Cognates include Middle Low German blosen, West Frisian bloazje, Old Swedish blusa, and with umlaut also Middle Low German blöschen, Old English blȳsian.

From Middle Dutch bleren, from Old Dutch *blerien, from Proto-Germanic *blarjaną, probably ultimately onomatopoeic. Cognate with German plärren. The Dutch vowel phoneme /ɛː/ is normally restricted to French borrowings and interjections. It must be due here to the onomatopoeic character of the word o
From Middle Dutch bōde, from Old Dutch bodo, from Proto-Germanic *budô.

From Middle Dutch boef, boeve, bouve, from Old Dutch *buovo, from Proto-Germanic *bōbô, a reduplicated form of *bō- (“father, brother, male relative”). Cognate with English bub, Pennsylvania Dutch Bub, German Bube, Icelandic bófi (“rogue, knave”). Related also to English babe, English boy.

From Middle Dutch boecstaef, boecstave, from Old Dutch buocstaf, *buocstavo, from Proto-Germanic *bōkastabô, *bōkastabaz (“letter, written symbol”), equivalent to boek + staaf. Compare German Buchstabe, English bookstave.
From Middle Dutch boesem, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bōsmaz.

From Middle Dutch bogen, further etymology uncertain, perhaps a Proto-Germanic *baugjan, which would probably be related to *baugijaną (“to bend”) and thus related to Etymology 2 below. Cognate only with Old Frisian bāgia.
From Middle Dutch bolc, from Proto-Germanic *bulnuka, perhaps related to the root of English bulk, referring to the convex shape.

parole.significato: a bur, a spiny cupule, often of a chestnut
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bolster, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz.

From Middle Dutch bund, from Old Dutch *bund, from Proto-Germanic *bundą; with ablaut formed as the same root as binden. The word could also be neuter until the 19th century, when it became increasingly common under the influence of German Bund.

From Middle Dutch bonc, bonck, bunck (“bone”), from Old Dutch *bunko, from Proto-Germanic *bunkô (“pile, heap, lump”). Cognate with West Frisian bonke (“bone”), Saterland Frisian Bunke (“bone”), German Low German Bunk (“bone”), Icelandic buna (“ox-bone”).
From Middle Dutch bône, from Old Dutch *bōna, from Proto-Germanic *baunō.
From Middle Dutch borstel, from Old Dutch *burstil, from Proto-Germanic *burstilaz.
From Middle Dutch breiden, from Old Dutch *bregdan, from Proto-Germanic *bregdaną.

parole.significato: broom, several plants of the subfamily Faboideae, particularly those (formerly) belonging to the genus Genista
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch breme, from Proto-Germanic *bremjō (“thorn bush”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem-, an extension of *bʰer- (“to stick out”), which would make it related to braam (“bramble”).

parole.significato: to snort (such as a horse or a pig)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch brieschen, further etymology unknown, but probably related to other similar sounding words such as brallen (“to brag, boast”), brommen (“to mumble, mutter”), bruisen (“to froth, form bubbles”), brullen (“to cry, roar”). Perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to bre

From Middle Dutch brine, from Old Dutch *brīni, from Proto-Germanic *brīniją, *brīną, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mrīno- (“salt, sea”), from *móri (“sea”). Compare Latin marīnus (“of the sea, marine”).

parole.significato: village green, functioning as a central square
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch brinc, from Old Dutch *brinc, from Proto-Germanic *brinkaz. Cognate with English brink.

parole.significato: to breed (especially by birds or oviparous animals)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch broeden, from Old Dutch *bruoden, from Proto-Germanic *brōdijaną.

From Middle Dutch bronst, earlier brunst, from Old Dutch *brunst, from Proto-Germanic *brunstiz, from *brinnaną (“to burn, to be on fire”) + *-stiz, the latter form the abstract noun former *-þiz (which became productive with stems ending in nasals), according to Kroonen from Pre-Germanic *bʰrénuh₁e
From Middle Dutch brudegōme, from Old Dutch brūdigomo, from Proto-Germanic *brūdigumô.

parole.significato: to form bubbles, to froth, to fizz
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bruuschen, from Old Dutch *brūskon, from Proto-Germanic *brūskōną, a variant of *brūsan (“to ferment, froth”), which could be an extension of Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to brew, boil”), or otherwise borrowed from a substrate.
From Middle Dutch bule, from Old Dutch *būla, from Proto-Germanic *būlijǭ, *būlǭ. Cognate with English beal, German Beule.
From Middle Dutch bucken, also bocken, from Old Dutch *bukken, from Proto-Germanic *bukkijaną, related to *beuganą (“to bend”).

parole.significato: bull (male bovine, or one of certain other male mammals)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bulle, from Old Dutch *bullo, from Proto-Germanic *bulô. Cognate with English bull.
From Middle Dutch bondel, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *bundil-, derivative of *bundą (“bundle”). Equivalent to binden + -el.
From Middle Dutch damp, from Old Dutch *damp, from Proto-Germanic *dampaz.
From Middle Dutch danc, from Old Dutch thank, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz.
From Middle Dutch dapper, from Old Dutch *dappar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz.
From Middle Dutch dat, from Old Dutch that, from Proto-Germanic *þat, neuter form of *sa. Cognate with German das, English that.

From Middle Dutch dau, dauwe, from Old Dutch *dāu, from Proto-Germanic *dawwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”). Compare Low German Dau, West Frisian dau, German Tau, English dew, compare also Danish dug.
From Middle Dutch dêel, from Old Dutch dēl, deil, from Proto-Germanic *dailą.
From Middle Dutch deken, from Old Dutch *thekina, from Proto-Germanic *þakinō.
From Middle Dutch delle (“valley; dune valley”), from Old Dutch della (“valley; (geography) depression; dune valley”), from Proto-Germanic *daljō. Cognate with English dell.
From Middle Dutch dêlen, from Old Dutch dēlen, from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną. Cognate with English deal.

parole.significato: to diminish, to dampen, to subdue, to dim, to make faint or less pronounced
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dempen, from Old Dutch *dempen, from Proto-Germanic *dampijaną (“to cause to smoke/emit vapour”).
From Middle Dutch derde, from Old Dutch thriddo, from Proto-Germanic *þridjô.
From Middle Dutch dertene, dertiene, from Old Dutch *thritēn, *thritien, from Proto-Germanic *þritehun. Compare West Frisian trettjin, German dreizehn, English thirteen, Danish tretten.
From Middle Dutch dertich, from Old Dutch *thrītig, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz.

From Middle Dutch dōghet, dōget, from Old Dutch *dugath, *dugeth, *dugith (“virtue”), from Proto-Germanic *dugunþō (“usefulness, virtue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to be ready, be sufficient”).

parole.significato: wooden dowel, small wooden peg in woodworking used for connecting pieces of wood
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *duevel (attested in the verb develen), from Old Dutch *duvil, from Proto-Germanic *dubilaz, probably derived from *dubjaną, whence English to dub. Cognate with Middle Low German dövel, Old High German tubil, whence modern German Dübel. English dowel may also be cognate; see there.
From Middle Dutch doeveke (“stopper”), formed from Proto-Germanic *dubilaz (“peg”) but with a different suffix.

parole.significato: that; referring to a thing or a person further away.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch die, a merger of Old Dutch thie, thē, thia, thiu and similar forms of the demonstrative. As in Old High German ther, der it replaced the original masculine and feminine nominative forms from Proto-Germanic *sa.
From Middle Dutch diefte, from Old Dutch *thiuvitha, *thiofta, from Proto-Germanic *þiubiþō. Equivalent to dief (“thief”) + -te. Cognate with English theft.
From Middle Dutch dienen, from Old Dutch thienon, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōną.
From Middle Dutch dienst, from Old Dutch *thionost, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz. Equivalent to dienen + -st.
From Middle Dutch diepde, diepte, from Old Dutch diupitha, from Proto-Germanic *diupiþō, from *deupaz (“deep”). Equivalent to diep + -te.
From Middle Dutch dî, from Old Dutch thī, from Proto-Germanic *þiz.
From Middle Dutch dijn, from Old Dutch thīn, from Proto-Germanic *þīnaz.

From Middle Dutch dinsendach. Probably from Proto-Germanic *þingas-dagaz (“Day of Thingsus”), from *þingą + *dagaz. Thingsus, Tiw or Týr was the name of the Germanic god of justice. Compare Low German Dingsdag and German Dienstag.
From Middle Dutch disch, from Old Dutch disk, from Proto-Germanic *diskuz (“table; dish; bowl”), from Latin discus. Cognate with English dish and German Tisch (“table”).

parole.significato: a drawing pole between the animals of team of a cart, particularly in relation to horse carts
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dissel, from Proto-Germanic *þinhslō.

parole.significato: a long, soft raceme, as of a cattail plant
parole.testo: Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *duttaz. Compare Old High German tutto, especially its derivate tuttokolbo (“cattail”).

From Middle Dutch doel, doele (“ditch that separated two fields”), from Old Dutch *duola, from Proto-Germanic *dōlijǭ, *dōlijō (“dale, valley”). Related to dal (“dale, valley”). Likely, the initial meaning was "ditch, pit" which shifted to "pile of earth" to "pile of earth used as target in a shooti
From Middle Dutch *dong, from Old Dutch *dunga, from Proto-Germanic *dungō. Cognate to English dung.
From Middle Dutch donker, dunker, from Old Dutch *dunkar, from Proto-Germanic *dunkalaz, *dunkaraz.
From Middle Dutch dôpe, from Old Dutch dōpa, from Proto-Germanic *daupō. Equivalent to a deverbal from dopen.
From Middle Dutch dōre, from Old Dutch thuro, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw.
From Middle Dutch derschen, darschen, dorschen, from Old Dutch *threscan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną.
From Middle Dutch drâet, from Old Dutch *thrād, from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz. Equivalent to draaien (“to turn”) + -d (“verbal noun”).

parole.significato: the act of bearing or wearing something
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dracht, from Old Dutch *draht, from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz. Equivalent to dragen (“to carry, wear”) + -t (“verbal noun”).

parole.significato: dregs of grains from brewing or refining
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch draf, from Old Dutch *draf, from Proto-Germanic *drabaz.
From Middle Dutch drāgen, from Old Dutch dragan, from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“draw, pull, carry”).
From Middle Dutch dranc, from Old Dutch *thrang, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwaz. Related to dringen (from Proto-Germanic *þrinhwaną). Cognate with English throng, German Drang, Norwegian trang.
From Middle Dutch dranc, from Old Dutch *drank, from Proto-Germanic *drankiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to pull; draw; sip”); compare German Trank (“drink; potion”).
From Middle Dutch drāven, from Old Dutch *thravon, from Proto-Germanic *þrabōną.
From Middle Dutch dreigen, from Old Dutch *threigen, of unclear origin. According to Pokorny, related to Proto-Germanic *þrinhwaną (“to force, push”).

parole.significato: to make vibrate, as with a pneumatic drill
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch drillen, from Old Dutch *thrillen, from Proto-Germanic *þriljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through, over”). Compare English thrill.
From Middle Dutch droom, from Proto-Germanic *þrumi, *dramjan, related to *þrumjaz (“disturbance, violence”). See also Old Saxon drom, Old English þrymm.
From Middle Dutch dronc, from Old Dutch *drunc, from Proto-Germanic *drunkiz (“drink”). More at drink.

parole.significato: drunk, drunken, in a state of intoxication after drinking alcohol beverages
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dronken, from Old Dutch druncan, from Proto-Germanic *drunkanaz.

From Middle Dutch drope (“drop”), from Old Dutch dropo, from Proto-Germanic *drupô. When unsuffixed, drop is more common than drup, but suffixed druppel is more common than droppel; this is likely due to the effects of i-umlaut triggered by the suffix -el. Indeed, drup is assumed to be based on drup

From Middle Dutch drutsate (“steward”), from a Common Germanic compound of Proto-Germanic *druhtiz (“troop”) and a derivative of Proto-Germanic *satjaną (“set”). Cognate with German Drost and Truchsess, Old Norse dróttseti.

From Middle Dutch *dusen, from Old Dutch *dūson, from Proto-Germanic *dūsōną, probably related to Proto-West Germanic *dwās (“stupid”). Not attested in Middle Dutch, but presumable derivatives are attested.
From Middle Dutch dulden, from Old Dutch tholon, from Proto-Germanic *þulāną, from Proto-Indo-European *telh₂-.

parole.significato: to doze, to nap, to sleep lightly
parole.testo: Unclear. May be from Middle Dutch dutten (“to rage”), through the semantic development: “rage” → “be out of one's mind” → “be unconscious” → “doze”, possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þeutaną (“to roar, howl”).
From Middle Dutch diere, dure, from Old Dutch diuri, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz. Doublet of dier.
From Middle Dutch dwerelen, from *dweren, from Old Dutch *thweran, from Proto-Germanic *þweraną. The change in vowel from e to a may have happened by analogy with warrelen.
From Middle Dutch echter, also efter, standing beside echt, from Old Dutch eft, from Proto-Germanic *aft-. Compare English eft, after.
From Middle Dutch *ēle, *ēelde, from Old Dutch *ili, from Proto-Germanic *ili (“sole of the foot”).

Reformed by epenthesis of -d- from Middle Dutch eerre, from Old Dutch *ēriro, from Proto-Germanic *airizô, an adjective formed from the comparative adverb *airiz. By surface analysis, eer (“ere, before”) + -er.

parole.significato: a drying oven, a drying kiln
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch eeste, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aistaz.

parole.significato: to give in ownership, to grant
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch eigenen, from Old Dutch *eiginon, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aiginōną. Equivalent to eigen + -en.
From Middle Dutch endeloes, from Old Dutch *endilōs, from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz, equivalent to einde (“end”) + -loos (“-less”).
From Middle Dutch ellef, elf, from Old Dutch *ellef, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Compare German elf, West Frisian alve, English eleven, Danish elleve.

parole.significato: elbow (joint between upper arm and forearm)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ellenbōge, from Old Dutch *elinbogo, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô.
From Middle Dutch elsene, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *alisnō, *alusnō. Related to *ēlō, whence Dutch aal, German Ahle, English awl.

parole.significato: not (often with another negator, see usage notes)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ne, en, from Old Dutch ne, from Proto-Germanic *ne, from Proto-Indo-European *né.

parole.significato: a tract of open, often raised agricultural land near or surrounding a village or hamlet
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch enc, ultimately from or related to Proto-Germanic *angraz (“meadow, lowland”).
From Middle Dutch enkel, ankel, from Old Dutch *enkal, *ankal, from Proto-Germanic *ankulaz.

From Middle Dutch anclau. There are two possible origins put forward: * A folk etymological interpretation of Proto-Germanic *ankulaz (“ankle, hip”), which descended separately into Dutch as enkel (“ankle”). * Equivalent to a compound of enkel (“ankle”) + klauw (“claw”), where the first part lost it
From Middle Dutch ēren, from Old Dutch *erien, from Proto-Germanic *arjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éryeti.
From Middle Dutch ernst, from Old Dutch ernost, from Proto-Germanic *ernustuz.

parole.significato: a tract of open, often raised agricultural land near or surrounding a village or hamlet
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch esche, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *atiska-. More at German Esch, Gothic 𐌰𐍄𐌹𐍃𐌺 (atisk).
From Middle Dutch etmael. Equivalent to et- + maal. The rare prefix derives from Proto-Germanic *idi-.

From earlier flard, flerd. Of obscure origin, but apparently related to West Frisian flarde, Saterland Frisian Fludde, German Low German Flarr (“patch”). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *flazdō.
Of uncertain origin. Perhaps a nasalized derivative of Proto-Germanic *flakurōną (“to flutter, beat repeatedly”).

parole.significato: a very large wooden vat in which beer is lagered
parole.testo: From Old Dutch *fuodar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą. Cognate with English fother, German Fuder, French foudre.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Unclear; Possibly; perhaps
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch focke, further origin unclear. Possibly from the verb vocken (“to blow”), itself of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Faroese fokka (“jib”), though this could have been a reverse borrowing. Both of these could be from Proto-Germanic *fuk(k)ōn- (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-Europe
From Middle Dutch gāve, from Proto-Germanic *gēbiz, cognate with Old Norse gæfr (“comfortable”), Danish gæv. Derived from the verb *gebaną (“to give”).

parole.significato: gale (any plant of the family Myricaceae)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gagel, from Old Dutch *gagal, from Proto-Germanic *gagulaz.

parole.significato: gallows, wooden framework on which persons are put to death by hanging
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch galge, from Old Dutch *galga, from Proto-Germanic *galgô, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰalg- (“long switch, rod, shaft, pole, perch”). Compare German Galgen, West Frisian galge, English gallows, Danish galge.

From Middle Dutch gouwe, gauwe (“quick, fast, hasty”), alteration of gâ, from Old Dutch gā, from Proto-Germanic *ganhuz, *ganhwaz (“sudden, quick”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Low German gau (“quick, fast”), German jäh (“sudden, abrupt”). More at gay.

parole.significato: Used with a verb stem to create a neuter uncountable noun referring to an action or its result, seen as a single collec…
parole.testo: From the prefix above with an 'empty' suffix originating from Old Dutch *-i, from Proto-Germanic *-ją.

parole.significato: Creates a neuter noun which refers to a mass or a collection of objects.
parole.testo: From ge- + Middle Dutch -te, from Old Dutch *-ti, from Proto-Germanic *-itją.
From Middle Dutch gebot, from Old Dutch gibot, from Proto-Germanic *gabudą. Compare German Gebot.
From Middle Dutch gedachte, from Old Dutch githāht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtaz.

parole.significato: to tolerate, to permit, to condone
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gedogen, from Old Dutch *gedōgen, from Proto-Germanic *gadaugijaną. Equivalent to ge- + dogen.
From Middle Dutch gedult, from Old Dutch githuld, from Proto-Germanic *gaþuldiz. Equivalent to a deverbal from dulden, gedulden. Compare German Geduld, more at German dulden.

parole.significato: no, not a, not an, not any
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch negeen, ne gene, (also as engheen, en geen), from Old Dutch chein, ghein, nehein (“not one; none”), ultimately corresponding to Proto-Germanic *nehw ainaz (“nor one”). Compare German kein, Yiddish קיין (keyn), English none.

From Middle Dutch geest, from Old Dutch *gēst, a nominalization of an adjective that meant “dry, infertile”, a derivation of Proto-Germanic *gais- (“infertile”), a root probably meaning "cracking, breaking, gaping;" see *gīnan. See also German gähnen. Cognate to West Frisian gaast, geast (as in the
From Middle Dutch gehuegen, from Old Dutch *gihuggen, from Proto-Germanic *gahugjaną. Equivalent to ge- + heugen.
From Middle Dutch geliken, from Old Dutch gilīkon, from Proto-Germanic *galīkōną. Equivalent to ge- + lijken.
From earlier gelove, from Middle Dutch gelôve, from Old Dutch gilōvo, from Proto-Germanic *galaubô.

parole.significato: to believe, to hold a belief
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gelôven, from Old Dutch gilōven, from Proto-Germanic *galaubijaną (“to believe, hold valuable”). Cognate with German glauben.
From Middle Dutch gelōven, from Old Dutch *gilovon, from Proto-Germanic *galubōną. By surface analysis, ge- + loven. Cognate with German geloben.
From Middle Dutch gemac, from Old Dutch *gimak, from Proto-Germanic *gamaką, a substantivised form of *gamakaz.
From Middle Dutch gemoeten, from Old Dutch *gimuoten, from Proto-Germanic *gamōtijaną.

From Middle Dutch genesen, from Old Dutch *ginesan, from Proto-Germanic *ganesaną, in which the Proto-Germanic *ga- prefix indicates completeness (perfectivity), and the Proto-Indo-European *nes- (“to return home”) recovery. The now-obsolete verb generen (“to provide for oneself”) is also derived fr
From Middle Dutch genuch, from Old Dutch *ginuog, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Cognate with West Frisian genôch, German genug, English enough, Low German noog, Swedish nog.
From Middle Dutch ghenot, from Old Dutch *ginot, from Proto-Germanic *ganutą. Related to genieten.

From Middle Dutch gerichte, gerechte (“court of law”), from Old Dutch *gerihte, from Proto-Germanic *garihtiją (“something prepared or arranged”). Compare Old English gerihte. The sense "dish" developed independently already in Old Dutch gerihte (“meal”). Cognate in both meanings: German Gericht.

From Middle Dutch gherecht, from Old Dutch *gereht (in gerehto), from Proto-Germanic *garehtaz, from *ga- + *rehtaz. Compare Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (garaihts), Old English geriht, German gerecht. Cognate in both meanings: German Gericht.
From Middle Dutch gereet, from Old Dutch *girēde, from Proto-Germanic *garaidijaz, prefixed form of Proto-Germanic *raidijaz, from Proto-Germanic *raidaz.
From Middle Dutch gering, from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *reng-ja, of obscure origin. Probably not related to wringen.
From Middle Dutch gerwen, from Old Dutch *gerwen, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną.

From Middle Dutch gêssle, gêsele. The atypical -s-, rather than -z-, points at Old Dutch *gēsl(a), where the -s- was directly followed by the -l-, instead of by a vowel, blocking the s → z sound change, from Proto-Germanic *gaisilaz, from *gaizaz (“spear”) + *-ilaz (suffix deriving names of tools).
From Middle Dutch geslachte, from slachte, from Old Dutch slahta, from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, related to *slahaną (“to hit, strike”), compare German Geschlecht (“gender, kind, lineage”).

parole.significato: a span, a team (pair or larger team of draught animals)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gespan (“clasp; chain, bracelet”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ga- *spannaną.

From Middle Dutch gesprec (“speaking, speech”), from Old Dutch *gisprekki, from Proto-Germanic *gasprakją. Equivalent to ge- + spreken. Its use as a term for “conversation” dates to early Modern Dutch, in this sense it ultimately displaced older gespraak. Compare Low German Gespreek, German Gespräch
From Middle Dutch gevoelen, from Old Dutch *gefuolen, from Proto-Germanic *gafōlijaną. Equivalent to ge- + voelen.
From Middle Dutch gewaet, from Old Dutch giwādi; ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wēdiz. The unprefixed form is still seen in the related compound lijnwaad. Unrelated to the verb waden.
From Middle Dutch geweldich, from Old Dutch *giweldig, composed of giwald + -ig. The base word descends from Proto-Germanic *gawaldiz. By surface analysis, geweld + -ig.

From Middle Dutch gewis, gewes (“certain, sure”), from Old Dutch *gewis (“certain, sure”) and gewisso (“certainly, surely”), both from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz (“known, sure”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know”). Cognate with English wis (“certain, sure”), German gewiss (“certain”), Danish

From Middle Dutch gewrochte (“produced thing”), from Old Dutch *giwurht, *giwurhti, from Proto-Germanic *gawurhtiją, *gawurhtiz, from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to work”). Cognate with Old English gewyrht, geweorht, Old Saxon giwurht, Old High German giwurht, Middle High German geworhte, gewurhte,
From Middle Dutch geselle, from Old Dutch gisello, from Proto-Germanic *gasaljô. Cognate with German Geselle.
From Middle Dutch ghesinde, from Proto-Germanic *gasinþiją, hence related to zenden (“to send”). Compare German Gesinde (“household”).
From Middle Dutch gir, gier, from Old Dutch *gīr, from Proto-Germanic *gīraz, related to *geraz (“greed, desire, coveting”).
From Middle Dutch ghier, from Proto-Germanic *jēzō, a derivation from *jestuz (“fermentation”). The -r is a result of rhotacism.

From Middle Dutch giselaer, giselare, from gisel (“hostage”, also “pledge, security”) + -aer. The former from Old Dutch *gīsel, from Proto-Germanic *gīslaz. Equivalent to archaic gijzel + -aar. The use of this suffix in a passive sense is comparable to martelaar (“martyr”). The proscribed sense “hos
From Middle Dutch gellen, from Old Dutch *gellan, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną.

parole.significato: yonder; there; used to indicate something that is not here
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ginder, from Proto-Germanic *jainar (“over there”). Cognate with English yonder.
From Middle Dutch gisteren, from Old Dutch *gestaron, from Proto-Germanic *gesteran.
From Middle Dutch glat, from Old Dutch *glad, from Proto-Germanic *gladaz.

From Middle Dutch glimmen, from Old Dutch *glimman, from Proto-Germanic *glimmaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to gleam, shimmer, glow”). See also Norwegian glim, dialectal Old Swedish glim, glimma.
From Middle Dutch gloet, from Old Dutch *gluod, from Proto-Germanic *glōdiz. Equivalent to gloeien (“to glow”) + -d (“verbal noun”).

Related to West Frisian gloppe (“alley”), Old Norse gloppa (“mountain gorge”), Norwegian Bokmål glop (“opening, hole”), Icelandic glopa, Faroese gloppa (“ajar”); per Kroonen, all from Proto-Germanic *gluppa (“open space”), a derivative of *gluppōn (“yawning, being open”), from Pre-Germanic *glub-n-,
From Middle Dutch gelve, from Proto-Germanic *gelbaną. Influenced by Late Latin colfus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).
From Middle Dutch gome, goom. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gaumaz, *gaumō (“attention”).

From Middle Dutch goor (“filthy”), from Middle Dutch goor, gore (“mud; dirt”), from Old Dutch *gor, from Proto-Germanic *gurą (“manure; filth”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer-. Cognate with Old High German gor, Old Norse gor, Old English gor (English gore).
From Middle Dutch gōte, from Old Dutch *gota, from Proto-Germanic *gutō. Cognate with German Gosse.
From Middle Dutch gorden, from Old Dutch gurden, from Proto-Germanic *gurdijaną.

parole.significato: canal (in a city, with houses on each side)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gracht, from Old Dutch *graft, *graht, from Proto-Germanic *graftuz. Equivalent to graven (“to dig”) + -t (“verbal noun”).
From Middle Dutch graf, from Old Dutch graf, from Proto-Germanic *grabą, *grabō (“grave, trench, ditch”).

parole.significato: to graze (to eat grass from a pasture)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch grasen, from Old Dutch *grason, from Proto-Germanic *grasōną, akin to modern gras (“grass”). More at graze.
From Middle Dutch grepe, from Old Dutch *gripi (“grasp, clutch”), from Proto-Germanic *gripiz. A variant nominative singular form, Old Dutch *grip, is preserved in begrip.
From Middle Dutch grepe, from Old Dutch *grēpa (“handle, grip”), from Proto-Germanic *graipō.
From gruppe + -el or denominative from gruppelen, both obsolete, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *grabaną (“to dig”). The vocalism is originally Flemish.

parole.significato: waterside area, overgrown with willows and reeds
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch grient, from Proto-Germanic *greuna-, a variant of *greutą (“grit, coarse sand”).

parole.significato: something small; a grain or crumb of something
parole.testo: Diminutive of gries (“grit, gristle”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *greutą, see also German Grieß, Old English greot.
From Middle Dutch grint, grinde, from Old Dutch *grinda, from Proto-Germanic *grindō (“sand, pebbles”).
From Middle Dutch groeve, grove, from Old Dutch gruova, from Proto-Germanic *grōbō. Doublet of groeve.
From Middle Dutch groeyen, from Old Dutch gruoien, from Proto-Germanic *grōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”). Cognate with English grow.
From Middle Dutch groeve, from Old Dutch gruova, from Proto-Germanic *grōbō. Doublet of groef.
From Middle Dutch grôte. Equivalent to groot + -te. A reinterpretation of earlier Middle Dutch grôte, from Proto-Germanic *grautį̄ (whence German Größe).

From Middle Dutch grûwen, grouwen, from Proto-Germanic *grūwijaną, with cognates in Middle High German and Old High German, but further origin unclear; perhaps ultimately an imitative derivative of Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”), or instead from *gʰer- (“to rub, stroke, grind”).

parole.significato: to think someone deserves something, to witness or acknowledge someone's success or enjoyment without envy or grudge (u…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gunnen, from Old Dutch *giunnan, from Proto-Germanic *gaunnaną, a prefixed form of *unnaną. Cognate with German gönnen.

parole.significato: her; third-person singular feminine objective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch haer, from Old Dutch hiro, from Proto-Germanic *hezōi.

parole.significato: her; third-person singular feminine possessive determiner
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch haer, from Old Dutch hira, from Proto-Germanic *hezōz.
From Middle Dutch haer, from Old Dutch hiro, from Proto-Germanic *hezǫ̂.
From Middle Dutch hagel, from Old Dutch *hagal, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz.
From Middle Dutch hacken, from Old Dutch *hackon, from Proto-Germanic *hakkōną.

parole.significato: ham (cured pork from the thigh of a swine)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch hamme, from Old Dutch *hama, from Proto-Germanic *hammō, from Proto-Indo-European *kónh₂m (“leg”).
From Middle Dutch hamel, from Old Dutch *hamal, from Proto-Germanic *hamalaz (“mutilated, castrated”). Cognate with German Hammel. Further origin uncertain; perhaps related to ham (“bacon”).
From Middle Dutch [Term?], from Old Dutch *handag, from Proto-Germanic *handugaz. Corresponds to hand + -ig.
From Middle Dutch hantwerc, from Old Dutch *handwerk, from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to hand + werk.

parole.significato: to malfunction, to be out of order, falter
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch haperen, of uncertain origin, but possibly from a derivation of Proto-Germanic *hamalōną (“to mutilate, hamper”).
From Middle Dutch harpe, from Old Dutch *harpa, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ.

Derived from Proto-Germanic *hainō (“grindstone”), similar to Low German heenk, Old Norse hein. Outside of Germanic, related to Latin cos (“grindstone”), Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “pinecone”), Middle Irish cath (“sharp-minded”).
From Middle Dutch hees, from Old Dutch hes, from Proto-Germanic *haisaz.
From Middle Dutch heiligen, from Old Dutch *hēlagon, *heiligon, from Proto-Germanic *hailagōną. Equivalent to heilig (“holy”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch helft, helfde, from Old Dutch *helvida, from Proto-Germanic *halbiþō.

parole.significato: him; third-person singular masculine objective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hem, from Old Dutch himo, from Proto-Germanic *himmai.

parole.significato: them; third-person plural objective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Old Dutch hin, from Proto-Germanic *himaz.

parole.significato: a herdsman, herd, herder of a flock of animals
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch herder, earlier herde from Proto-Germanic *herdō (“herd”) + agent suffix -e; the agent suffix -er replaced -e when the latter fell in disuse as signifying agency.

From Middle Dutch hermelijn, a diminutive of hermel, harmel, from Old Dutch *hermilo, itself also a diminutive, of *harmo, from Proto-Germanic *harmô. By surface analysis, hermel + -lijn; hermel (also harmel) survived into early Modern Dutch. Cognate with Middle Low German hermelīn, German Hermelin.

parole.significato: it; third-person singular neuter subjective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch het, hit, from Old Dutch it, hit, from Proto-Germanic *it, *hit.

From Middle Dutch hoevel, huevel, hovel, huffel, from Old Dutch huvil, from Proto-Germanic *hubilaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kewb- (“to bend; a bend, joint”), see also Proto-Germanic *hupiz (“hip”), *hufą (“elevated place, hill”). Cognate with Middle Low German hovel, Old High German hu
From Middle Dutch hiele, from Old Dutch *hela, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz.
From Middle Dutch hinderen, from Old Dutch *hindaron, from Proto-Germanic *hinderōną.

From Middle Dutch hitte, from Old Dutch *hitta, from Proto-Germanic *hitjō; see *haitį̄. Cognate with German Hitze and Yiddish היץ (hits). Now commonly interpreted as heet (“hot”) + -te (“ness”). Also related with English heat.
From Middle Dutch hoe, from Old Dutch huo, from Proto-Germanic *hwō.
From Middle Dutch hoef, from Old Dutch *huof, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Cognate with West Frisian hoef, German Huf, English hoof, Danish hov.
From Middle Dutch hoere, from Old Dutch *huora, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ.

parole.significato: to cough, push air from the lungs forcefully, as because of a cold
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hoesten, from Old Dutch *huoston, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną, derived from the strong verb *hwōsaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s-.
From Middle Dutch hoeve, from Old Dutch *huova, from Proto-Germanic *hōbō (“plot of land”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Probably; ipotesi scartata nel testo
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch homme, identical to homme (“mold”), of uncertain origin, but probably related to Old Norse húm (“dusky, twilight”), from Proto-Germanic *skim- (“to shine-”), which has been compared to Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover”), but according to the Etymologisch Woordenboek this is

parole.significato: an old unit of area measuring 100 roeden, approximately 0.14 hectares
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hont, from Old Dutch *hunt, from Proto-Germanic *hundą. Related to honderd.
From Middle Dutch hondert, from Old Dutch *hundert, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą.

From Middle Dutch gondrave (various spellings attested), where the first element is *gont (from Proto-Germanic *gundaz (“sore, boil, canker”); may not have existed as simplex in Middle Dutch) and the second is a by-form of Middle Dutch reve (“vine”) (see Proto-West Germanic *rebā); this refers to th
From Middle Dutch hongerich, from Old Dutch hungerig, from Proto-Germanic *hungragaz, *hungrugaz (“hungry”), equivalent to honger + -ig. Compare German hungrig, English hungry.
From Middle Dutch honinch (“honey”), from Old Dutch honing, from Proto-Germanic *hunangą. Cognate with English honey and German Honig.

parole.significato: home, place where one belongs, shelter
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch honc (“corner, nook”), likely through Old Dutch from Proto-Germanic *hunk-, *hank-. Cognate with East Frisian Low German Hunk (“house”) and perhaps with the Old High German name Hancwin. Likely related to haak (“hook”) and hoek (“corner”). Perhaps also comparable to Alemannic Germa
From Middle Dutch hôoi, from Old Dutch *hōi, variant of houwi, from Proto-Germanic *hawją.
From Middle Dutch hone, hoon, from Old Dutch *hōna, *hōni, from Proto-Germanic *hauniz.
From Middle Dutch hôop, from Old Dutch *hōp, from Proto-Germanic *haupaz.
From Middle Dutch hose, from Old Dutch *hosa, from Proto-Germanic *husǭ.

From Middle Dutch hoppe, from Old Dutch *hoppo, from Proto-Germanic *huppô (“hops”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keup (“tuft, hair of the head”), referring to the plant's appearance. Compare Old Saxon hoppo, Old High German hopfo, Middle English hoppe.

parole.significato: botfly, insect of the family Oestridae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch horsel, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hursulǭ. Cognate with French frelon.
From Middle Dutch hout, from Old Dutch holt, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz.

parole.significato: to bail, to scoop water out of a boat, cellar etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch osen, from Old Dutch *ōsan, from Proto-Germanic *ausaną. The initial h- is a hypercorrection first attested in early modern Dutch, possibly by analogy with hoos.

parole.significato: to squat, to bend (through the knees)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hūken, from Proto-Germanic *hūkaną (“to squat”), from *hūkkan-, back-formed from the iterative *huk(k)ōn-, from Proto-Indo-European *kuk-néh₂, from *kewk- (“to curve, bend”) (also the source of English high).

Likely onomatopoeic. Appears to contain the frequentative suffix -eren. An early etymology suggesting that it may ultimately represent a derivation from Proto-Germanic *heufaną (via an unattested Middle Dutch *hūven) is today generally dismissed as implausible.
From Middle Dutch hulpe, from Old Dutch hulpa, from Proto-Germanic *hulpiz.

parole.significato: shell, case (usually cylindrical covering part of an item, in particular of ammunition)
parole.testo: Related to Swedish hylsa, English holster, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hulisō, cognate with Proto-Germanic *huljaną.
From Middle Dutch huwen, from Old Dutch *hīwen, from Proto-Germanic *hīwijaną, related to *hīwą (“marriage”).

From Middle Dutch *îwe f (attested as uwe and ieve, the latter being a conflation with the unrelated word for “ivy”), from Old Dutch *īwa, from Proto-Germanic *īwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw-. Cognate with German Eibe, English yew.
From Middle Dutch *ile, from Old Dutch *īla, from Proto-Germanic *īlō.
From Middle Dutch iseren, iserijn, from Old Dutch īsarnīn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarnīnaz. By surface analysis, ijzer + -en.
From Middle Dutch inganc, from Old Dutch *ingang, from Proto-Germanic *inngangaz, ultimately from *ǵʰengʰ-. Equivalent to in (“in”) + gang (“passageway, hallway”).
From Middle Dutch inlichten, from Old Dutch *inliuhten, from Proto-Germanic *inliuhtijaną. Equivalent to in (“in”) + licht (“light”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch ja, from Old Dutch *jā, from Proto-Germanic *ja.
From Middle Dutch jakken, from Old Dutch *jakkon, from Proto-Germanic *jakkōną.
From Middle Dutch jammer, from Old Dutch iāmer, from Proto-Germanic *jēmaraz (“miserable, sorrowful”).
From Middle Dutch joghet, juegt, from Old Dutch jugint, jugethe, from Proto-Germanic *jugunþiz, from earlier *juwunþi.

parole.significato: gout, a metabolic disease which painfully inflames the joints
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch jicht, from Old Dutch *jiht, *giht, from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz.

parole.significato: you; second-person singular subjective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ji, northern form of gi, from Old Dutch gī, from Proto-Germanic *jīz, a northwest Germanic variant of *jūz, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs. Cognate with Low German ji, jie, English ye, West Frisian jimme, German ihr. Until the earlier 20th century, jij was considered exclusively co
Diachronically from Middle Dutch jongelinc, from Old Dutch iungelig, from Proto-Germanic *jungilingaz. By surface analysis, jong + -ling.
From Middle Dutch joc, juc, from Old Dutch *juk, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm. Compare German Joch, West Frisian jok, English yoke, Danish åg, Swedish ok.

From Proto-Germanic *kekǭ, *kēkǭ, *kakǭ, *kaukǭ, *keukǭ (“jaw; palate; pharynx”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁- (“to chew”). Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Sooke (“cheek”), West Frisian tsjeak (“jaw”), English cheek, Swedish käke (“jaw; jowl”), Norwegian kjake (“jaw”), Old Norse kók (“m

parole.significato: a (now usually benevolent) tiny folkloric bearded man who traditionally wears a pointy red hat, lives in harmony with n…
parole.testo: Possibly already from Middle Dutch. Equivalent to a compound of koof (from Middle Dutch kove, from Old Dutch *kovo, from Proto-Germanic *kubô (“hut, shed”)) and a less certain second element that might be hou (“friendly, favorable disposition”). Related to German Kobold. For sense 2, compare with En
From Middle Dutch keiser, from Old Dutch keiser, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet with tsaar (“tsar”).

parole.significato: to turn around, to turn around an axis
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch keren, from Old Dutch kēren, from Proto-Germanic *karzijaną, *kaurijaną.
From Middle Dutch kerne, from Old Dutch *kerno, from Proto-Germanic *kernô, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂-n-on-, *ǵr̥h₂nóm, related to *kurną (“corn, grain”).

parole.significato: kettle, cauldron (a pot used to boil water)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ketel, from Old Dutch *ketil, from Proto-Germanic *katilaz, from Late Latin catillus.

From Middle Dutch clateren. Cognate with Low German klateren, English clatter and perhaps dialectal Norwegian Nynorsk klatra (“to beat, pound”); from Proto-Germanic *klatrōjaną, but ultimately onomatopoeic.
From Middle Dutch clauwe, from Old Dutch *klawa, from Proto-Germanic *klawō. Compare German Klaue, English claw, Danish klo.
From Middle Dutch clouwen, from Old Dutch *clouen, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną; a doublet of klooien and equivalent to klauw + -en.
From Middle Dutch clêet, from Old Dutch clēth, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą. Cognate with German Kleid, Luxembourgish Kleed, English cloth.
From Middle Dutch clepel, cleppel, from Old Dutch *klepil, *kleppil, from Proto-Germanic *klapilaz, *klappilaz. Equivalent to klappen or kleppen + -el.
From Middle Dutch clingen, clinken, from Old Dutch *clingan, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą (“to sound”).

parole.significato: to nail, to rivet, to clinch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch clingen, clinken, from Old Dutch *clingan, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą (“to adhere to, cling to”).

parole.significato: rock or cliff in or around sea water
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch clippe, from Old Dutch *klippa, from Proto-Germanic *klippō. See klif (“cliff”), which probably shares the same ultimate origin.
From Middle Dutch cloec, from Old Dutch *cluoc, from Proto-Germanic *klōkaz. Compare German klug for the "clever" sense.

From Middle Dutch clompe (“lump or mass of metal, wooden shoe, clump”), from Old Dutch *klumpo, from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“lump, clump, mass; clasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *glembʰ- (“clamp, mass”). Cognate with Old Frisian klumpa, English clump, Low German Klump, German Klumpen. Related to cl
From Middle Dutch clôyen (variant of clouwen), from Old Dutch *clōien (variant of *clouen), from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną; possibly related to klooi and a doublet of klauwen.
From Middle Dutch clôot, from Old Dutch *klōt, from Proto-Germanic *klautaz. Cognate with English cleat. Related to Dutch kluit (“lump; lump of earth”) and klont (“lump”).
From Middle Dutch cloven, causative form of Middle Dutch clieven, from Old Dutch *clievan, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną. Akin to English cleave.

From Middle Dutch cluft, clucht, from Old Dutch *kluft, from Proto-Germanic *kluftiz (whence also German Kluft, English cleft). Equivalent to klieven (“to cleave”) + -t (“verbal noun”), and the Middle Dutch meaning was at first "separation, department", later also "neighbourhood of a town". The sens

parole.significato: a ball of thread or yarn, a clew
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cluwen, from Old Dutch *kliuwīn, from Proto-Germanic *kliuwīną, *klewô, from Proto-Indo-European *glew-. Cognate with English clew.

From Middle Dutch cnijf, from Old Dutch *knīf, from Proto-Germanic *knībaz. Related to Dutch knijpen (“to pinch”). Cognate with English knife, Low German Knief, Luxembourgish Knäip, Swedish kniv, Old Norse knífr.
From knikken, from Proto-Germanic *knikkoną (“to fold, snap”), which is imitative.
From Middle Dutch knobbe, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *knappô (“button”), one of many kn- words related to *knuttô (“a knot”). Compare regional German Knubbel as well as Knopf (“button”).

parole.significato: button (knob or small disc serving as a fastener)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cnôop, from Old Dutch *knōp, from Proto-Germanic *knaupaz, one of several kn- words related to *knuttô (“knot”). Cognate with German Knauf.

parole.significato: a knob, roundish handle, ornament etc.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *knappô, or a variant of it, one of many kn- words related to *knuttô (“a knot”). Cognate with German Knopf and probably English knop. Also related with Dutch knob, knobbel, German Knubbel, which are cognate with English knob.

From Middle Dutch cnudde, Old Dutch *knotto, from Proto-Germanic *knuttan-, *knuttô. Related to knod, English knot, West Frisian knotte, Middle High German Knotze, German Knoten, Danish knude, Norwegian knute, Swedish knut, etc.

From Middle Dutch codde (“testicle, club”), from Proto-Germanic *kuddô, and ultimately Proto-Indo-European *geu (“to curve, to bend”); same source as Old Armenian կոր (kor), Lithuanian gurnas (“ankle, hip, bone”), and Norwegian kaure (“curly lock of hair”). Cognate to Low German Koden (“belly, paunc
From Middle Dutch coeke, from Old Dutch *kuoko, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô. Doublet of quiche.

parole.significato: cog (clinker-built, flat-bottomed sailing cargo ship of the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cogghe, from Proto-Germanic *kuggō (compare German Kogge (“cogboat”), Swedish kogg (“cogboat”)), from Proto-Indo-European *gugā (“hump, ball”) (compare Lithuanian gugà (“pommel, hump, hill”)), from *gēu- (“to bend, arch”).

parole.significato: white spot on the forehead of a horse or a cow
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *kullaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“head”).
From Middle Dutch comst, from Old Dutch cumst, from Proto-Germanic *kumþiz. Equivalent to komen (“to come”) + -st (“verbal noun”). Distant doublet of base and basis, via Proto-Indo-European *gʷḿ̥tis.
From Middle Dutch cont, from Old Dutch cunt, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz.
From Middle Dutch koninghdom, from Old Dutch *kuningduom, from Proto-Germanic *kuningadōmaz. Equivalent to koning + -dom. Cognate with English kingdom, German Königtum, West Frisian keuningdom.
From Middle Dutch côop, from Old Dutch *cōp, from Proto-Germanic *kaupaz. See the verb kopen (“to buy, trade”).

From Middle Dutch cote, from Proto-Germanic *kutō-, related to *kautōn- (“knuckle”), of unknown ultimate origin, with no certain cognates outside of Germanic. However, compare kuil (“hole in the ground”) and keutel (“hard animal dropping”), though Kroonen considers comparisons with the latter a stre
From Middle Dutch crage, from Proto-Germanic *kragan- (“throat”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ-, which could be related to Ancient Greek βρόχθος (brókhthos, “throat”).
From Middle Dutch crabben, further from Proto-Germanic *krabbōną, with a geminated variant of the stem in Proto-Germanic *krabitaz, whence Dutch kreeft (“lobster”).

From Middle Dutch cratte (“basketware, mold”), from Old Dutch *kratta, *kratto (“basket”), from Proto-Germanic *kratjô, *krattijô (“basket”), from Proto-Indo-European *gred-, *gre(n)t- (“plaiting, wicker, basket, cradle”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to bind, twist, wind”).
From Middle Dutch cruepel (“lacking, missing”), from Old Dutch *krupil, from Proto-Germanic *krupilaz. Cognate with German Krüppel, English cripple.
From Middle Dutch crimpen, from Old Dutch *crimpan, from Proto-Germanic *krimpaną.
From Middle Dutch kring, from Old Dutch *kring, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz.
From Middle Dutch cronkelen, from Proto-Germanic *krunkōną.

From Middle Dutch croes, ultimately from the root of kroezen (“to be tightly curled”), from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of hair”).

parole.significato: an unhealthy enlargement of a bird's gullet
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crop, from Old Dutch *krop, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz. Doublet of groep. Cognate with English crop, German Kropf.

parole.significato: to form or have formed an ice shove or ice jam
parole.testo: A contraction of kruiden (“to push”), from Middle Dutch cruden, from Old Dutch *crūdan, from Proto-Germanic *krūdaną, *kreudaną. Cognate with English crowd.

parole.significato: a curl shape (such as in hair or writing)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crulle, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“that which is curled”), from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of hair”).

parole.significato: to give out a dry and brief cough
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cuchen, coechen, cochen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kuh- (“to cough”), likely of onomatopoeic origin. Akin to English cough, German keuchen.
From Middle Dutch cule, from Old Dutch *kūla, from Proto-Germanic *kūlō, related to *kūlǭ (“hole”).
From Middle Dutch cume (“barely; almost”), from Old Dutch, from Proto-Germanic *kūma- (“pitiful, dear”). Cognate to German kaum (“barely”) and come in English comely.
From Middle Dutch conde, cunde, from Old Dutch *kundi, from Proto-Germanic *kundīn (“being known”), derivation with grammatical change from *kunþaz (“known”).

From Middle Dutch cunst, const, cunste, conste (“skill, ability, knowledge, craft”), from Old Dutch *kunst (“knowledge, know-how, skill”), from Proto-Germanic *kunstiz (“knowledge, ability”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”), equivalent to kunnen + -st. Cognate with Old Saxon kunst (“ski
From Middle Dutch cust, from Old Dutch *kust, from Proto-Germanic *kustuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus. Equivalent to kiezen (“to choose”) + -t (“verbal noun”).
From kwakken (“to dump, to throw, to smack”), from Proto-Germanic *kwakōną, probably ultimately imitative. Related to Old English cwacian.

From Middle Dutch quackele, from *kwakila (compare Low German Quakkel), blend of *kwak (“quack”) and Proto-Germanic *hwahtilō (“quail”) (compare dialectal Dutch wachtel, German Wachtel), diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *kʷoḱt- (compare Latin co(c)turnīx, Lithuanian vaštaka, Sanskrit चातक (cātaka,
From Middle Dutch quast, from Old Dutch *kwast, from Proto-Germanic *kwastuz.
From Middle Dutch quinen, from Old Dutch quīnan, from Proto-Germanic *kwīnaną (Proto-West Germanic *kwīnan).
From earlier lade through regular syncope of intervocalic -d- (compare weer, blij, broer), from Middle Dutch lāde, from Old Dutch *latha, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþō.
From Middle Dutch lâge, from Old Dutch *lāgi, from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz.
From Middle Dutch lâge, from Old Dutch *lāga, from Proto-Germanic *lēgō, derived with ablaut from the stem of *ligjaną (“to lie, rest on”).
From Middle Dutch laen, lane, from Old Dutch *lana, from Proto-Germanic *lanō. More at lane.

From Middle Dutch laer, from Old Dutch lār, hlār (only in place names), from Proto-Germanic *hlēraz or *hlēzaz, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- and related to Latin clarus (“bright, clear”). The etymology is unclear, and the word is rare in the languages where it is found, in an
From Middle Dutch laet, from Old Dutch *lāt, from Proto-Germanic *lētaz.
From Middle Dutch laf, from Proto-Germanic *laba-, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Cognate with German laff (“slack, insipid”).

parole.significato: woollen broadcloth (fulled and woven fabric made of wool), very sought-after for clothing in the feudal era
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lāken, from Old Dutch lacan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“linen, cloth”).
From land + Middle Dutch ouwe, a variant of ooy, which ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *awjō; more at Ooij.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: a rag, a piece of cloth
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lap, lappe, from Old Dutch lap, from Proto-Germanic *lappa-, *lappô (“rag, cloth”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Cognate with German Lappen.
From Middle Dutch last, from Old Dutch *last, from Proto-Germanic *hlastuz. Equivalent to laden (“to load”) + -st (“verbal noun”).
From Middle Dutch lêet, from Old Dutch *lēth, from Proto-Germanic *laiþą, related to *laiþaz (“loath”). Unrelated to lijden (“to suffer”).
From older ledig, from Middle Dutch lēdich, from Old Dutch *lithig, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.
From Middle Dutch leen, from Old Dutch *lēn, from Proto-Germanic *laihną.
From Middle Dutch leesten, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laistijaną. Cognate to English last, German leisten.

parole.significato: loin, bottom part of the back
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lenden, from Old Dutch lendin, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄.
From Middle Dutch lengen, from Old Dutch *lengen, from Proto-Germanic *langijaną. Equivalent to lang (“long”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and, like lengte, shows the effect of historical umlaut.

From Middle Dutch lengede, from Old Dutch *lengitha, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō. Corresponds to lang + -te with umlaut (compare lengen). Cognate with German Low German Längde, Längd, Längte, Längt (“length”), English length, Scots lenth, lainth (“length”), Saterland Frisian Loangte (“length”), Wes
From Middle Dutch letten, from Old Dutch *letten, from Proto-Germanic *latjaną. Equivalent to laat (“late”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.
From Middle Dutch loteren, from Proto-Germanic *lutiran, possibly related to *lūtaną (“to bend”). Cognate with English loiter. See also leut (“fun”).
Possibly from Proto-Germanic *lusi-, which would then be ablautically related to *lausaz (“loose”). The sense would have evolved from "replacement of the guard" to "watchword."
From Middle Dutch lit, let, leet, from Old Dutch *lid, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz.
From Middle Dutch liet, from Old Dutch *lioth, from Proto-Germanic *leuþą.
By surface analysis, lief + -lijk. Diachronically, from Proto-Germanic *leubalīkaz. Cognate with German lieblich, Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (liubaleiks).
From Middle Dutch geliken, liken, from Old Dutch *gilīkon, from Proto-Germanic *galīkōną.
From Middle Dutch lijnwaet; the first element is lijn (“flax”), the second derives from Proto-Germanic *wēdiz, whence also gewaad.

From Middle Dutch lindeworm, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *linþawurmiz. Equivalent to a tautological compound of linde (“snake”) + worm (“snake”). Cognate to English lindworm, German Lindwurm, Old Norse linnormr (“constrictor snake”), Norwegian lindorm (“serpent”), Danish lindorm.

parole.significato: luff, windward side of a sail or ship. (no plural)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *loef, from Old Dutch *luof, from Proto-Germanic *lōf-, from Proto-Indo-European *lāp-, *lēp-, *lep- (“flat”). Although attested only very late, its origin in Old Dutch is relatively certain as Old French borrowed lof from it. Cognate, with various inflectional variants, with Middl
Inherited from Middle Dutch loeyen, inherited from Old Dutch luoien, inherited from Proto-Germanic *hlōaną.

With dialectal (eastern) -oe- from Middle Dutch luren (“to look sharp”), from Proto-Germanic *lūraną, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“to see”), similar to loens (“cross-eyed”), Latin luscus (“half-blind”). Compare German lauern, English lour and lurk.
From Proto-Germanic *lumpa-, related to *limpaną (“to glide, go, hang loosely”), similar to German Lumpen (“tatter, rag”).
From Middle Dutch longe, also longen, longene, from Old Dutch *lungan, *lunganna, from Proto-Germanic *lunganjō.

parole.significato: any plant of the genus Allium; leek
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch look, from Old Dutch *lōc, from Proto-Germanic *laukaz. Compare Low German look, Look, German Lauch, English leek, Danish løg, Swedish lök. More at leek.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laum-, perhaps related to *lamaz (“withered, lame”). Compare the verb lummelen (“to lounge about”).

parole.significato: a sprout, shoot, stem etc. growing on an existing plant part
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lote, from Old Dutch *lōt, from Proto-Germanic *lōda, related to *landa- and *leudaną (“to grow, sprout, shoot up”).

From Middle Dutch louter, variant of luyter, lûter, lutter, from Old Dutch *lūtir, luttir, from Proto-Germanic *hlūtraz. The -ou- is probably due to influence by late Middle High German lauter, older lūter, from Old High German hlūter, from the same Germanic source. Compare modern German lauter.

From Middle Dutch loy, from Proto-Germanic *lujaz. further etymology unsure. May be cognate with the Old Norse adjective lúinn (“exhausted”). Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewH- (“to cut off, separate, free”), source of Proto-Germanic *lausaz, Albanian lirë.
From Middle Dutch ludere, from Old Dutch *lūthara, from Proto-Germanic *lūþaru.
From Middle Dutch māget, from Old Dutch *magath, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs. Doublet of meid.

From Middle Dutch mael, male, from Old Dutch māla, from Proto-Germanic *mēlō (“young cow”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)melh₁-. Compare Old Irish míl (“animal”), Ancient Greek μῆλον (mêlon, “lamb”), Breton mil (“animal”).

parole.significato: a poppy, any of several plants of genus Papaver
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch maencop. The first element derives from Proto-Germanic *mōhô; the current form was altered by folk etymology. Equivalent to maan + kop.

parole.significato: agricultural meadow used for hay, hayland
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch made, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *maþwō, *mēþwō.

From Middle Dutch mager, from Old Dutch *magar, from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Cognate with German, Danish, and Swedish mager, etc., and with Latin macer, Italian magro and English meager through Indo-European.
From Middle Dutch malsch, from Old Dutch *malsc, from Proto-Germanic *malskaz.
From Old Dutch *manon, from Proto-Germanic *manōną.

parole.significato: the acute, highly contagious viral disease measles
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch masel (“sore, spot on the skin”), from Old Dutch *masala, from Proto-Germanic *masalō. Compare English measles.

Compound of mee (“madder”) + krap (“hook”). The first element is inherited from Middle Dutch mede, which derives from Proto-Germanic *maiþǭ. The second element was likely added in reference to hook-shaped parts of the plant. First attested as meecrappe in 1588, although Middle Dutch already has crap
From Middle Dutch meit, variant of meget, from Old Dutch *megith, *magath, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs. Doublet of maagd.
From Old Dutch *meinēth, from Proto-Germanic *mainaiþaz (“perjury”), from *mainą + *aiþaz.
From Middle Dutch merrie, from Old Dutch *meria (compare Old High German meriha), from Proto-Germanic *marhijō. Cognate with West Frisian merje, German Mähre, English mare.
From Middle Dutch met, from Proto-Germanic *matją, whence also German Mett (through Low German). Related with Proto-Germanic *matiz, whence English meat.

Originally muyck (“repository for apples and pears”), assumed to be related to muik (“soft”), as in "place where fruit ripens and becomes soft," from Proto-Germanic *meukaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mewg- (“slimy, slippery”).
From Middle Dutch middel, from Old Dutch middil, from Proto-Germanic *midil-, *midlą, *midilą, *medalą (“middle”). Cognate with English middle, Low German Middel and German Mittel.
From Middle Dutch miere, from Old Dutch *miuri, from Proto-Germanic *miurijǭ.

parole.significato: me; first-person singular objective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mi, from Old Dutch mī, from Proto-Germanic *miz.

parole.significato: to think to oneself, ponder, muse
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mimeren, from Old Dutch *mīmrōn, from Proto-Germanic *mīmrōną (“to think, have in mind, care for”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *smer- (“to fall into thought, remember, care for”). Cognate with Old English mimorian (“to remember, keep in mind”). More at remember.
From Middle Dutch mite, from Old Dutch *mīta, from Proto-Germanic *mītōn.
From Middle Dutch micken, from Old Dutch *mikken, from Proto-Germanic *mikjaną.
From Middle Dutch milde, from Old Dutch mildi, from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz.
From Middle Dutch milte, from Old Dutch *milta, from Proto-Germanic *meltǭ.
From Middle Dutch minre, from Old Dutch minniro, from Proto-Germanic *minnizô, comparative of adjective deriving from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small”).
From Middle Dutch mis-, from Old Dutch mis-, from Proto-West Germanic *missa-.

From Middle Dutch misdaet, from Old Dutch *misdād (“misdeed”), from Proto-Germanic *missadēdiz < *missa- (“mis-”) + *dēdiz (“deed, act”). Equivalent to mis- + daad or misdoen (“to misdo”) + -d (“verbal noun”). Cognate with Old Saxon misdād (“misdeed”), German Missetat, West Frisian misdied, English

parole.significato: nauseous, nauseated, having the urge to vomit
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch misselijc (“diverse, confused”), from Old Dutch *missilīk, from Proto-Germanic *missalīkaz. Analysable as mis (“wrong”) + -e- + -lijk.
From Middle Dutch missen, from Old Dutch *missen, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *meyt-.
From Middle Dutch mist, from Old Dutch *mist, from Proto-Germanic *mihstaz.
From Middle Dutch modder (“filth”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz. Cognate to German Low German modder (“mud”).
From Middle Dutch moedich, from Old Dutch *muodag, from Proto-Germanic *mōdagaz; equivalent to moed + -ig.

Probably related to Old Dutch *mocha (“piece, lump”), from Proto-Germanic *mukkan- (“bump, lump”), perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *muk- (“heap”), similar to Ancient Greek μύκων (múkōn, “pile”). Compare Old English mūga, Old Norse múgr (“mass, heap (of corn)”).
From Proto-Germanic *mulmaz. Cognates: see Old Norse malmr.
From Old Dutch *munda, from Proto-Germanic *mundō.

parole.significato: morning gift (the gift given by the bridegroom to the bride on the morning after the wedding night)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch morgengave, from Old Dutch *morgangāva, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō, equivalent to morgen (“morning”) + gave (“gift”).

From Middle Dutch moude, from Old Dutch *molda, from Proto-Germanic *muldō, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to rub, grind”). Cognate with German Molte (“dust, earth”), English mold, Old Frisian molde (“earth, soil”), Old Norse mold (“earth”), Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌻𐌳𐌰 (mulda, “earth, clay”).

parole.significato: an animal's mouth and muzzle or snout
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch muul, from Old Dutch mūl, from Proto-Germanic *mūlą.

From Middle Dutch murwe, morwe, variant forms of meru, merwe (“soft, tender, weak”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *marwaz. Cognate with German mürbe, Old English meru, mearu (“soft, tender”). More at mellow.

parole.significato: Used to negate the pronoun or adverb which follows it, yielding the same part of speech
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ne, en, from Old Dutch ne, from Proto-Germanic *ne.

parole.significato: a seam, as where pieces of textile are sewn together
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch naet, from Old Dutch *nād, from Proto-Germanic *nēdiz (“seam”). Equivalent naaien (“to sew”) + -d (“verbal noun”).
From Middle Dutch nave, from Old Dutch *nava, from Proto-Germanic *nabō.
From Middle Dutch nâyen, from Old Dutch *nāien, from Proto-Germanic *nēaną.

parole.significato: nude, not wearing any clothing; can also apply to part of the body with exposed hide
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch naket, naect, from Old Dutch nakot, from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked, bare”). Cognate with Low German naakd, German nackt, English naked, West Frisian neaken, Danish nøgen, Swedish naken.
From Middle Dutch naest, from Old Dutch *nāist, *nāst, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”).

parole.significato: to draw near, to approach, to be imminent
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nâken, from Old Dutch nāken, from Proto-Germanic *nēkijaną.
From Middle Dutch nap, from Old Dutch nap, from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz.
From Middle Dutch nauwe, from Old Dutch nauw, from Proto-Germanic *hnawwaz.
From Middle Dutch navele, navel, from Old Dutch *navalo, from Proto-Germanic *nabalô.
From Middle Dutch neen, nee, from Old Dutch *nēn (“none, not one”), from *ne ēn, from Proto-Germanic *ne + *ainaz.
From Middle Dutch nete, from Old Dutch *nita, from Proto-Germanic *hnitō.
From Middle Dutch neghentien, from Old Dutch *niguntēn, *niguntien, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun. Compare West Frisian njoggentjin, German neunzehn, English nineteen, Danish nitten.
From Middle Dutch nesse, from Old Dutch nesse, from Proto-Germanic *nasją. Equivalent to an ablauting secondary form of neus (“nose”).
From Middle Dutch net, nette, from Old Dutch *net, *netti, from Proto-Germanic *natją, from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to turn, twist, knot”).
From Middle Dutch nēvel, from Old Dutch *neval, from Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos.
From Middle Dutch nie, from Old Dutch nie, from Proto-Germanic *ne *aiwaz. Cognate to German nie. Equivalent to n- (“n-”) + ie (“ever”) (from Middle Dutch ie, from Old Dutch io).
From Middle Dutch niere, from Old Dutch *nioro, from Proto-Germanic *neurô, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷʰrós.
From Middle Dutch nieten, from Old Dutch nietan, from Proto-Germanic *neutaną.

parole.significato: a water spirit, especially one who lures (young) people to drown; a neck, nix, nixie
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nicker (“nix, nixie; demon”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *nikwus, *nikwis (“nix, water-sprite”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“to wash”).
