From Middle Dutch noch, from Old Dutch noh (“until now, still”), from Proto-Germanic *nuh (“still”, literally “now too”), from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”) + *-kʷe (“and, also”).
From Proto-Germanic *naudīgaz (compare English needy and German nötig). By surface analysis, nood + -ig.
From Middle Dutch noemen, from Old Dutch *nuomen, from Proto-Germanic *nōmijaną.

From Middle Dutch nocke, possibly ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *hnakkô (“back of the neck”); the meanings "neck", "top", "hook" all merged into each other. Likely related to English nock and nook; see there for more, as well as Faroese nakkur (“steep promontory”).

From Middle Dutch nootdruft, nootdurft. It is a tautological compound of nood (“need”) + druft (“need”). The second element, found in Modern Dutch only (in metathesized form) in this compound, derives from Proto-Germanic *þurftiz. Compare Gothic 𐌽𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌿𐍂𐍆𐍄𐍃 (naudiþaurfts).
From Proto-Germanic *nautą (“foredeal, profit, property, livestock”).
From Middle Dutch nu, from Old Dutch nū, from Proto-Germanic *nu.
From Middle Dutch nutte (“useful”), from Proto-Germanic *nutiz (“useful, useable, profitable”), from *neutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to seize; grasp; use”). Equivalent to nut + -ig.
From Middle Dutch ochtent, earlier ochte, from Old Dutch *ūhto, from Proto-Germanic *unhtwǭ. Compare regional German Uchte, Old English ūhta.
From Middle Dutch oefenen, an iterative of Middle Dutch oeven, from Old Dutch *uofnon, from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną.

parole.significato: bank (as in riverbank), shore (e.g. of a lake)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch oever, from Old Dutch *uovar, from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz. Cognate with German Ufer.
From Middle Dutch of, ofte. In Middle Dutch the two words merged; the form of derives from Old Dutch of, from Proto-Germanic *jabai.
From Middle Dutch ofte, from Old Dutch *oftho, from Proto-Germanic *efþau. Cognate with Old Saxon eftha, Old Norse eða.
From Middle Dutch odelijc, from ode (“easy, light”) + -lijc. The first element is also found in ootmoed and derives from Proto-Germanic *auþuz.
From Middle Dutch ommegang, from Old Dutch *umbigang, from Proto-Germanic *umbigangaz. Equivalent to om (“around”) + gang (“course, way”), or a deverbal from omgaan.
From Middle Dutch on, from Old Dutch *āna, from Proto-Germanic *ēnu (“without”), from Proto-Indo-European *anew, *enew (“without”).

From Old Dutch ungilīk, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, on- (“un-”) + gelijk (“equal”). Compare Old English unġelīċ (English unlike), German ungleich, Old Norse úlíkr (see there for North Germanic descendants).

From Middle Dutch onrecht, from Old Dutch unreht, from Proto-Germanic *unrehtaz. The noun represents an early nominalization of the neuter singular of the adjective; compare for example Old English unriht.

parole.significato: us; first-person plural objective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ons, from Old Dutch uns, from Proto-Germanic *uns, *unsiz.
From Old Dutch *unsa, from Proto-Germanic *unseraz.

parole.significato: Forms inchoative verbs, indicating that a process is beginning.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ont-, from Old Dutch int-, from Proto-Germanic *in-.
From Middle Dutch ontbinden, from Old Dutch antbindan, from Proto-Germanic *andabindaną. Equivalent to ont- + binden.

From Middle Dutch ontginnen, derived with prefix ont- from Proto-Germanic *ginnaną, which is not attested in unprefixed form in any Germanic language (compare beginnen and Old Dutch aginnan). Cognate to Old English onginnan and Old Saxon andginnan.

From earlier onweder, from Middle Dutch onweder, from Old Dutch *unwedar, from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą. Equivalent to on- + weer (literally “unweather”). Cognate with English unweather, German Unwetter, Swedish oväder.

20th century coinage. Compound of Middle Dutch ooy (“ait, island, wetland”) + bos (“forest”), the former being derived from Proto-Germanic *awjō and identical to the toponym Ooij. Unrelated to modern ooi (“ewe”).

parole.significato: A stork, bird of the family Ciconiidae.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch odevare. Related to Low German adebar, West Frisian earrebarre, all possibly from Proto-Germanic *ōdaborǭ or *ōdaborą.

parole.significato: opinion, judgement (conclusion of an act of deciding)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ordeel, from Old Dutch urdēl, from Proto-Germanic *uzdailiją. Equivalent to oor- + deel. Cognate with German Urteil, English ordeal. More at ordeal.

From Middle Dutch orloge, from Old Dutch *urlage. In this word, two Germanic words merged, both having the prefix ur- (modern Dutch oor- and oer-, with the former kept in compounds like oorzaak (“cause, driver”) and oorsprong (“origin”), and the latter borrowed from German). The first word was deriv
From Middle Dutch ootmoet, omoet, odemoede, from ode (“easy, light”) + moet (“boldness, courage”) (whence moed). The first element is also found in olijk and derives from Proto-Germanic *auþuz.
From Middle Dutch op, from Old Dutch up, from Proto-Germanic *upp.
From op + beuren. From Middle Dutch bueren, from Old Dutch *burien, from Proto-Germanic *burjaną. Cognate with Middle Low German upboren and Danish oppebære (“receive, collect (money)”).

parole.significato: to effervesce, to bubble up, to froth, to fizz
parole.testo: From op + bruisen, from Middle Dutch bruuschen, from Old Dutch *brūskon, from Proto-Germanic *brūskōną.
From Middle Dutch osse, from Old Dutch *osso, earlier *ohso, from Proto-Germanic *uhsô.
Possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *uberfullaz; equivalent to over- + vol.
From Middle Dutch parc, from Old Dutch *parruk, from Proto-Germanic *parrukaz (“enclosure, fence”). Doublet of perk.

parole.significato: a small coin, usually made of silver but later also of gold; penny
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch penninc, from Old Dutch pennink, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz.
From Middle Dutch pitte, from Proto-Germanic *pittan (compare dialectal German Pfitze (“pimple”)), oblique of Proto-Germanic *piþō.
From Middle Dutch ploech, from Old Dutch *pluog, from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz. The sense “team” originally derives from the team of animals drawing one plough.

parole.significato: wall plug (used to hold nails and screws)
parole.testo: From early modern plugge, from Middle Dutch *plugge, from Old Dutch *pluggi, from Proto-Germanic *plugjaz, of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps from the same source as plag (“cut-out sod”), itself considered to be from a substrate. Despite being attested only very late, it has certain cognates
From Middle Dutch poc, pocke, from Proto-Germanic *pukkaz, *pukkǭ (“pock; swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bʰew- (“to grow; swell”).

From Middle Dutch praten, further etymology unknown, but probably related to Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“boastful talk”). Cognates are found only in German Low German proten (East Frisian). English prate, prattle and the various Scandinavian verbs were borrowed from these two languages.

From Middle Dutch priem, from Proto-Germanic *preumaz (compare Low German Preen, German Pfriem), alteration of *preunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *brewn- (compare Lithuanian briaunà ‘edge’, Albanian brez ‘belt, girdle’).

parole.significato: to display, to show off (with the intention of making an impression)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pronken, perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *brahtaz, similar to pracht (“splendor”), Swedish prakt (“glory, pomp”) (loaned from Low German). See also German Prunk (“splendor”).

parole.significato: to puff, blow out (hot air, such as the chugging of a steam engine)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch puffen, sharing an imitative Proto-Germanic base with Old English pyffan, Middle English puffen, English puff. Compare Middle Low German puffen.

From Middle Dutch puut (“frog”), from Old Dutch pūt, from Proto-Germanic *put-, *pud- (“to swell”). Compare dialectal English pod (“belly”), pout (“a kind of fish”), Swedish puta (“to pout”). Akin to French bouder.

From Middle Dutch ram (“a male sheep”), from Old Dutch *ram, of West-Germanic origin, possibly from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“strong”). Cognate to English ram (“a male sheep”). The sense "battering ram" was borrowed as a semantic loan from Latin ariēs in Middle Dutch.

From Middle Dutch ramen (“to aim, to strive for, to guess”), possibly from Old Dutch *rāmon, from Proto-Germanic *rēmijaną, *rēmāną, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to set in motion, move about”), as in English roam.
From Middle Dutch rant, from Old Dutch *rant, from Proto-Germanic *randaz.
From Middle Dutch rāpen, from Old Dutch *rapon, from Proto-Germanic *hrapōną.
From Middle Dutch rasch, from Old Dutch *rasc, from Proto-Germanic *raskuz. Cognates include English rash, German rasch.
From Middle Dutch ratelen, ultimately of imitative origin. Compare German rasseln, English rattle. Possibly from a Proto-Germanic *hratōną (with frequentative suffix -elen).
From Middle Dutch rēde, from Old Dutch retha, from Proto-Germanic *raþjǭ (“reasoning, account”).

parole.significato: shipowner, executive of a shipping business
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch reder, agent noun from rêden (“to make ready”), from Proto-Germanic *raidijaną. By surface analysis, reden + -er.
From Middle Dutch regendrop, from Old Dutch *regandropo, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to regen (“rain”) + drop (“drop, droplet”).
From Middle Dutch rēkenen, from Old Dutch *recanon, from Proto-Germanic *rekanōną, indirectly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-.

A merger of two related verbs: * Middle Dutch rinnen (“to flow, to run fast”), from Old Dutch *rinnan, from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną. * Middle Dutch rennen (“to run/ride fast”), from Old Dutch *rennen, from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną. Doublet with runnen (“to manage”).

From Middle Dutch reude, possibly from Proto-Germanic *hruþjô (“large dog, hound”), itself possibly from *hruttōną (“to roar”), from a Proto-Indo-European root shared by Ancient Greek κόρυζα (kóruza), Old English hrot. Or, from Proto-Germanic *hreutaną, *hrūtaną, *hruttōną (“to snore”), which would

parole.significato: lard (fat from the abdomen of a pig)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch reusel, from Proto-Germanic *rusilą. Cognate with Old Saxon rusal, Old English rysel, West Frisian riezel. More distantly related to Danish ros, dialectal Norwegian Bokmål ros, rys.
From Middle Dutch ribbe, from Old Dutch *ribba, from Proto-Germanic *ribją.
From Middle Dutch rijcdom, rijcdoem, from Old Dutch *rīkdōm, *rīktuom, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijadōmaz, equivalent to rijk + -dom. Cognate with English richdom.
From Middle Dutch rijm, ripe, from Proto-Germanic *hrīmô.
From Middle Dutch rimpel, from Proto-Germanic *hrimpila-, related to *hrimpaną (“to fold, wrinkle”).

parole.significato: a rod, woody branch or staff, notably as a symbol of authority
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch roede, from Old Dutch ruoda, from Proto-Germanic *rōdō. Cognate with German Rute, Old English rōd (English rood).
From Middle Dutch roeyen, from Old Dutch *ruoien, from Proto-Germanic *rōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁-.

From Middle Dutch roem (“boasting”), from Old Dutch *ruom, from Proto-Germanic *hrōmaz (“noise, shouting”), related also to Proto-Germanic *hrōþiz with a change to a dental consonant, of IE origin. Compare German Ruhm (“fame”) and Old English hrēmiġ (“exultant”).
From Middle Dutch roer, from Proto-Germanic *rauzą (“tube”). Cognate with German Rohr. The modern Dutch -oe- instead of expected -oo- is unexplained.

parole.significato: soot (fine dark particles of amorphous carbon and tar, produced by the incomplete combustion of organic material or fue…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch roet, from Old Dutch *rōt, from Proto-Germanic *hrōtaz (“soot”).

From Middle Dutch rochge, rogge, possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz (“rough”), referring to the fish's texture. Cognate with Middle Low German roche, ruche, Old English reohhe, ruhha, German Rochen.
From Middle Dutch rōge, from Old Dutch *rogan, from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz.
From Middle Dutch romp, from Proto-Germanic *rumpa-, which could be related to *hrimpaną (“to wrinkle”). Also compare Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti (“to chop”).
From Middle Dutch rōden, from Proto-Germanic *rudōną. Cognate with German roden, (aus)rotten.
Inherited from Middle Dutch rôoc, from Old Dutch *rōk, from Proto-Germanic *raukiz.
From Middle Dutch rouwen, ruwen, from Old Dutch *riuwan, from Proto-Germanic *hrewwaną.

From Middle Dutch ruuch, ru, rou, from Old Dutch *rūh, *rū, from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz, *rūhwaz. The original stem ended in -h-, which disappeared between vowels, giving *rū- in the inflected forms in Old Dutch. This then gave rise to an alternative uninflected form *rū, which developed into Middle
From Middle Dutch rumen, from Old Dutch *rūmen, from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną. Derived from the adjective *rūmaz and/or the noun *rūmą, from which Dutch ruim. Cognate of räumen.

From Middle Dutch ruusschen, from Old Dutch *rūskon, from Proto-Germanic *rūskōną (“to rustle”), ultimately imitative. Cognate with German rauschen, Middle Low German rûschen, English rush. The now obsolete sense “to make noise” was due to confluence with unrelated druisen (whose unexpected -s- inst
From Middle Dutch runt, from Old Dutch *rund, from Proto-Germanic *hrunþaz.

parole.significato: a caterpillar, the larva of a butterfly
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rupse, from earlier rupsene, from Proto-Germanic *rūpō and probably related to *raupijaną. Related to German Raupe and West Frisian rûp.
From Middle Dutch ruste, from Old Dutch *rusta, from Proto-Germanic *rustijō. Cognate with English rest, German Low German Rüst (“rest”), German Rüste (“end, sunset”).

From Middle Dutch ruuch, ru, rou, from Old Dutch *rūh, *rū, from Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz. The original stem ended in -h-, which disappeared between vowels, giving *rū- in the inflected forms in Old Dutch. This then gave rise to an alternative uninflected form *rū, which developed into Middle Dutch ru

Borrowed, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sahsą (“stone chip, knife”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). The word also existed in the sixteenth century, but became obsolete and was borrowed again.
From Middle Dutch scale, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *skēlō, related to *skaljō (“husk, shell”). Cognate with German Schale (“bowl”).
From Middle Dutch scalm, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skalmō (“handle”). Cognate to Low German schalm, Saterland Frisian schalm, and possibly Old Norse skalm.

From Middle Dutch schape (“form”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skapą (“shape, nature, condition”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to split, cut”). Cognate with English shape (“form”), Middle High German geschaf (“creature”), Icelandic skap (“state, condition, temper, mood”). Related to Dutc
From Middle Dutch schare, from Old Dutch skara, from Proto-Germanic *skarō. Cognates include German Schar, English share.
From Middle Dutch scharren, from Old Dutch *skerran, from Proto-Germanic *skerraną, *skersaną.

From Middle Dutch schateren, scateren, from Old Dutch *skateron, from Proto-Germanic *skat-. Probably ultimately onomatopoeic in origin. Cognate with Low German schateren, English shatter and scatter. Related to schetteren.

parole.significato: shive, i.e. fragment of the woody core of flax or hemp
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch scēve, from Proto-Germanic *skibō-; cognate with Low German Schääv, German Schäbe, and English shive, all ‘fragment of the woody core of flax or hemp’.
From Middle Dutch schelden, from Old Dutch skeldan, from Proto-Germanic *skeldaną.
From Middle Dutch scillen, from Old Dutch skillen, from Proto-Germanic *skiljaną (“to split, cut, divide”). Related to verschil (“difference”) and English skill.

From Middle Dutch scellen, from Old Dutch skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellan, *skaljan, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skel-, from *kelh₁- (“to call, to shout, to make noise, to sound”) with an extra s-mobile.
From Old Dutch *skilling, from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz.
From Proto-Germanic *skankô with archaic diminutive suffix -el. Cognate with German Schenkel and English shank.
From Middle Dutch scherve, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *skarfaz, related to *skeraną (“to cut”).
From Middle Dutch sc(h)ore (“crack, rip, tear”), scure, from Proto-Germanic *skuriz, *skuraz, related to *skeraną (“to cut”). Cognate with English score.

From Middle Dutch schōren, from Proto-Germanic *skurō (“incision; tear; rift”), which is related to *skeraną (“to cut”). By surface analysis, scheur + -en. See also English score, Old Norse skor (“to tear”).

From Middle Dutch schicht, from Old Dutch *skiht, from Proto-Germanic *skihtiz, derived from *skehaną (from which geschieden). The meaning was "something that shoots forward" and is only attested in Dutch; the German near-cognate Geschichte preserves the earlier meaning "forward movement" and hence
From Middle Dutch schiere, from Old Dutch *skīr, from Proto-Germanic *skīriz.
From Middle Dutch schier, from Old Dutch scieri, from Proto-Germanic *skairiz.
From Middle Dutch schijn, from Old Dutch *skīn, from Proto-Germanic *skīnaz. Cognate with German Schein, English shine.
From Middle Dutch schim, schem, from Old Dutch *skim, *skimo, from Proto-Germanic *skimaz, *skīmô (“shine; light”). Related to schemeren.

From Middle Dutch schimmel (“rust”), from Proto-Germanic *skimla-, probably related to *skīnaną (“to shine”), referring to the dull shine of a fungal layer or its white color. Cognate with German Schimmel, whence is borrowed the sense “grey horse” (due to the similar colour).
Inherited from Middle Dutch schoeyen, inherited from Old Dutch *skuoion, inherited from Proto-Germanic *skōhōną, from Proto-Germanic *skōhaz. Doublet of schoen (“shoe (footwear)”, noun).
From Middle Dutch schoffel (“shovel”), from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *skuflō. Equivalent to schuiven + -el.

parole.significato: to travel around in freedom without a plan or profession, to wander
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch scooyen, from Proto-Germanic *skawjaną, which could be related to *skēwijaną (“to walk, go”). Related to Swedish skoja (“to joke”), borrowed from West Germanic.
From Middle Dutch schoot, from Old Dutch *skōt, from Proto-Germanic *skautaz.

parole.significato: a shovel, a spade, a digging tool
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schoppe, from Old Dutch *skuppa, from Proto-Germanic *skupjō. Probably from the same source as schoep (“blade of a water wheel”).

parole.significato: kick (strike with or raise the foot or leg)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schuppen (“to shove away”), from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną.
From Middle Dutch schouwen, from Old Dutch skouwon, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁-.
From Middle Dutch screde, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *skriþiz or *skridiz. Compare *skrīþaną (“to walk, crawl”), whence schrijden. Cognate with German Schritt.

parole.significato: to yell; to bellow; to shout; to talk loudly
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schrêwen, from Old Dutch *skrēwon, from Proto-Germanic *skraiwōną. Related to Dutch schreien.

parole.significato: to be startled, to get a scare
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schricken, from Old Dutch *skrikken, from Proto-Germanic *skrikjaną; the ultimate origin is uncertain, possibly related to *skeraną (“to shear”) or *skrīaną (“to scream”). Also compare Old Norse skaga (“to jut out”).
From Middle Dutch *schrinken, from Old Dutch *scrinkan, from Proto-Germanic *skrinkwaną. It is now rare; modern use may have been reinforced by English shrink.

parole.significato: a boat or small ship, usually a flat-bottomed one used for inland navigation or less commonly for coastal navigation; a…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schute, from Old Dutch skūta. Cognate with Middle Low German schûte (“a type of boat or light ship”). Perhaps tied to Proto-Germanic *skeutaz (“quick”), thus making it related to Old Norse skúta (“a small craft or cutter”), Old Norse skjótr (“quick”), Old English sċēot (“quick, rea

From Middle Dutch schorf with paragogic -t (cf. burcht), derived from Proto-Germanic *skurfa-, derived in turn from the verb *skerfan-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). See also scherf, scherp; also with Middle Low German schorf, Old High German scorf, German Schorf, Old English sceorf,
From Middle Dutch schutten, from Old Dutch *scutten, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”). Cognate with English shut.
From Middle Dutch schutter, schuttre, schotter, scuttere, alteration of earlier schutte, scutte (“shooter”), from Old Dutch *scutto, from Proto-Germanic *skutjô.

From tsedert, a variant form of sedert (pronounced with initial z-), from Middle Dutch seder (“thenceforth, since then”). Originally a Hollandic dialectal form, the other dialects used sider (which would have become modern *sijder(t)), from Old Dutch sīther, from Proto-Germanic *sīþiz (“later”), a c
From Middle Dutch slachten, from Old Dutch *slahton, from Proto-Germanic *slahtōną, related to *slahaną (“to hit, strike”). Cognate with German schlachten.

From Middle Dutch slecke, slacke, from Old Dutch *slecco, from Proto-Germanic *slikkô, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sliǵ-ōn, from *sley- (“smooth; slick; sticky; slimy”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Schleek, German Low German Slacke, Slack (“snail”).

parole.significato: snake, squamate of the suborder Serpentes
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch slange, from Old Dutch slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô (“snake, serpent”).
From Middle Dutch slanc, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *slinkaną (“to crawl, creep”). Compare German schlank.

From Middle Dutch slap, from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”). Cognate with German schlaff and schlapp.
From an earlier meaning of “simple, ordinary, inferior, plain” (cf. slechts), from Middle Dutch slecht (“smooth, flat”), from Old Dutch *sleht, from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz.

parole.significato: sled, sleigh, wheelless vehicle which glides on land or ice
parole.testo: From older slede, from Middle Dutch slēde, from Old Dutch *slido, from Proto-Germanic *slidô.
From Middle Dutch slegge, from Old Dutch *slegga, from Proto-Germanic *slagjǭ.

parole.significato: to pull, to drag, to tow (usually in a careless or unrefined manner)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sloren, sluren, of uncertain origin, but possibly related to Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, limp, slack”).
From Middle Dutch slijc, from Old Dutch *slīk, from Proto-Germanic *slīką, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sley- (“smooth; slick; sticky; slimy”). Compare English slick and slime.
From Middle Dutch slijm, from Old Dutch *slīm, from Proto-Germanic *slīmą. Cognate with German Schleim.
From Middle Dutch slicken, from Old Dutch *slikkon, from Proto-Germanic *slikkōną.
From Middle Dutch slingen, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną (“to worm, twist”). Cognate to English sling, German schlingen.

parole.significato: to shrink, to lessen, to decrease
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch slinken, from Old Dutch *slinkan, from Proto-Germanic *slinkaną.
From Middle Dutch slocken, from Proto-Germanic *slukkēn-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lug-.
From Middle Dutch slope, from Old Dutch *slōpa, from Proto-Germanic *slaupǭ.
From Middle Dutch slôpen, from Old Dutch *slōpen, from Proto-Germanic *slaupijaną.
From Middle Dutch slot, from Old Dutch *slot, from Proto-Germanic *slutą, related to the verb *sleutaną (“to lock”). Cognate with German Schloss and Schluss.

From Middle Dutch sluuc (“limp”), of uncertain origin. Possibly related to English slouch, which could be from Proto-Germanic *slakaz (“slack, weak”); or otherwise *slūm- (“slack, flabby”). Also compare sluimeren (“to slumber”) and the root of German schlau.

From Middle Dutch smade, from Proto-Germanic *smēhijaną (“to despise, belittle”) , from Proto-Indo-European *smēyg- (“small, thin, delicate”). See also Old Norse smá (“to scorn”), Proto-Germanic *smikraz (“fine, fair”).

From Middle Dutch smachten, ultimately from a variant of Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“small, little”). See also Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “a little of”), Latin mica. West Germanic cognates include Old High German gismāhtōn (modern German schmachten).
From Middle Dutch smal, from Old Dutch smal, from Proto-Germanic *smalaz. Cognate with English small, German schmal, Old Norse smalr, Gothic 𐍃𐌼𐌰𐌻𐍃 (smals).
From Middle Dutch smeer, from Old Dutch smero, from Proto-Germanic *smerwą. Cognate with English smear.

From Middle Dutch smelten, a merger of two Old Dutch verbs: * *smeltan, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną, a strong intransitive verb. * *smelten, from Proto-Germanic *smaltijaną, weak causative of the above.
From Middle Dutch smetten, smitten, from Old Dutch *smitton, from Proto-Germanic *smitjōną. Equivalent to smet + -en.

From Middle Dutch smitse, reformed from earlier smisse by analogy with smit (modern smid), from Old Dutch *smiththa, from Proto-Germanic *smiþjǭ. The development *-þj- > -ss- is also found in wisse, while *-þþ- becomes -tt- in lat, mot.
Possibly related to dialectal smuigen (“to act insidiously”), from Proto-Germanic *smeuganą.

The ending -ent is generally considered to be identical to eend (“duck”); the origin of smi- is however uncertain. Some link it to Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“small”), wigeons being fairly small of stature compared to, say, mallards.

parole.significato: to smother, to suffocate, to deprive of oxygen
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch smoren, from Proto-Germanic *smurōną (“to suffocate, strangle”), probably related to *smallijan (“to burn”) or Old English smoca (“smoke”).
First attested 1691, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *smīlijaną.
From Middle Dutch snavel, from Old Dutch *snaval, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz.
From Middle Dutch sneewit, from Old Dutch *snēwīt, from Proto-Germanic *snaiwahwītaz. Cognate with English snow-white.
From Middle Dutch snoer, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *snōrō, related to *nēaną (“to sew”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin”).; compare Gothic 𐍃𐌽𐍉𐍂𐌾𐍉 (snōrjō).

From Middle Dutch snôde, from Old Dutch *snōthi, from Proto-Germanic *snauþuz (“bald, naked, poor”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksnéw-tu-s, from the root *ksnew- (“to scrape, sharpen”). Cognates include German schnöde and Old Norse snauðr.
From Middle Dutch snotte, from Old Dutch *snotto, from Proto-Germanic *snuttuz.
From earlier spade, from Middle Dutch spade, from Old Dutch *spado, from Proto-Germanic *spadô.
From earlier spade, from Middle Dutch spade, from Old Dutch *spādi, from Proto-Germanic *spēdiz. Cognate with German spät.

parole.significato: a spoke, part between the center and outer rim of a wheel etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch spake, an Ingvaeonic form of the more usual speke, from Old Dutch *spēka, from Proto-Germanic *spaikǭ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“sharp point”).
From Middle Dutch spade, from Old Dutch *spado, from Proto-Germanic *spadô.
From Middle Dutch spâde, from Old Dutch *spādi, from Proto-Germanic *spēdiz (“late”).

parole.significato: to strain, to put tension on
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch spannen, from Old Dutch *spannan, from Proto-Germanic *spannaną.
From Middle Dutch sparen, from Old Dutch *sparon, from Proto-Germanic *sparōną.

From Middle Dutch speecsel, formed from older spekel by analogy with terms suffixed with -sel. The form spekel is from Old Dutch *spēkila, from Proto-Germanic *spaiklō. From the same root as spuwen. Cognate with German Speichel.
From Middle Dutch spellen, from Old Dutch *spellon, from Proto-Germanic *spellōną.
From Middle Dutch spueren, sporen, from Old Dutch *spurien, from Proto-Germanic *spurjaną.
From earlier spien, from Middle Dutch spien, from Old Dutch *spion, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną. The -d- was inserted by back-forming the present from the weak past spiede.

From Middle Dutch spier (“pointed object; blade of grass; long pole; muscle”), from Old Dutch *spīr, from Proto-Germanic *spīraz, *spīrǭ. In Middle Dutch, the word took the meaning "muscle", likely due to the similarities in shape between its earlier meanings and muscle fibers.
From Middle Dutch spoele, from Old Dutch *spuola, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ.

From Middle Dutch spoke, spooc, from spoke, spoocke, spoicke (“wizardry, witchcraft”), from Proto-Germanic *spōk. Further etymology unclear. Cognate with Middle Low German spôk, Low German spôk, Middle High German Spuch, and German Spuk.
From Middle Dutch spor, from Old Dutch *spor, from Proto-Germanic *spurą, from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-.
From Middle Dutch spot, from Old Dutch *spot, from Proto-Germanic *spuþþaz.
From Middle Dutch spotten, from Old Dutch *spotton, from Proto-Germanic *sputtōną. Equivalent to spot + -en.
From Middle Dutch spuwen, from Old Dutch *spīwan, *spiuwan, from Proto-Germanic *spīwaną.
From Middle Dutch sprekere, an alteration (due to change in suffix) of Old Dutch *spreko, from Proto-Germanic *sprekô (“speaker”), equivalent to spreken + -er.
From Middle Dutch springen, from Old Dutch *springan, from Proto-Germanic *springaną.
From Middle Dutch spruten, from Old Dutch *sprūtan, from Proto-Germanic *sprūtaną, *spreutaną.
From Middle Dutch stael, from Old Dutch stāl, from earlier *stahal, from Proto-Germanic *stahlą. Cognate with German Stahl, Danish stål, Icelandic stál, English steel, West Frisian stiel.
From Middle Dutch stadich, stedich, from Old Dutch *stādig, from Proto-Germanic *stēdīgaz. Cognate with German stetig, English steady.
From Middle Dutch stanc, from Old Dutch stank, from Proto-Germanic *stankwaz.
From Middle Dutch stapel, perhaps ultimately from a lost derivative of Proto-Germanic *stapiz (“step, stride”), referring to an insect that moves by jumps and strides.

parole.significato: always, continually, all the time, every time, each time
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stedes, steeds, an adverbial genitive of stede (“steadfast, durable”), with umlaut from the more common stade, from Old Dutch *stādi, from Proto-Germanic *stēdi-. Cognate with German stets.

parole.significato: an alleyway; a lane (between walls, fencing, etc.); a bystreet
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch steech, stege, from Old Dutch steyga, *stega (“stairway”), from Proto-Germanic *stigǭ (“staircase; ladder”). Cognate with Middle Low German stēge, Old High German stega. More distantly related to Old High German steiga (from Proto-Germanic *staigō-) and German Steg (from Proto-Germ

From Middle Dutch stekel, from Proto-Germanic *stiklaz, *stikilaz (“sting, stinger, peak, cup, goblet”), related to the verb *stikaną (“to stick”). Cognate with English stickle, Icelandic stikill, Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐌹𐌺𐌻𐍃 (stikls) (whence Russian стекло́ (stekló, “glass”), Lithuanian sti̇̀klas).

parole.significato: stilt (either of two poles with footrests that allow someone to stand or walk above the ground)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stelte, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *staltijǭ, which is related to *stalljan (“to place, put”)
From Old Dutch *stēnin, from Proto-Germanic *stainīnaz, equivalent to steen + -en.
From Middle Dutch stenig, from Old Dutch *stēnag, *steinag, from Proto-Germanic *stainagaz, equivalent to steen + -ig. More at stony.

parole.significato: one of the two ends of a ship's hull; the bow or the stern
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stēvene, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *stamniz (“tree stalk”).
From Middle Dutch stichten, from Old Dutch stiften, stihten, from Proto-Germanic *stiftijaną.

parole.significato: a bull; a male of certain mammals, in particular bovines
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stier, from Old Dutch stier, from Proto-Germanic *steuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros. Doublet of tauros.

From Middle Dutch stype, from Proto-Germanic *stīfa, from Proto-Indo-European *steyp- (“stiff, erect”), see also Latin stīpō, Latin stipulor, English stiff. Related to Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, the source of stijf (“stiff, rigid”).

parole.significato: to come to a stop, halt
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *stukkōną (“to stop, stick”).
From Middle Dutch stompe, from Old Dutch *stump, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz (“stump”). Cognate to German stumpf.
From Middle Dutch stout, from Old Dutch *stolt, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz.

From Middle Dutch strac (“tight, taut”), from Old Dutch *strak, from Proto-Germanic *strakaz, *strakkaz (“straight, tight, tense”), from Proto-Indo-European *streg-, *treg- (“stiff, rigid”). Cognate with Middle Low German strac (“tight, taut”), Old English stræc (“firm, strict, rigorous, unyielding”

From Middle Dutch strenge, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *strangijaz (“tight, tense”), *strangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut”). Compare German streng, English strong, Danish streng.

parole.significato: string, twined object, as most ropes or cords
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *strangiz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ-. Compare Low German Strenge, German Strang, English string, Danish streng.
From Middle Dutch strēven, from Old Dutch *strivon, from Proto-Germanic *stribōną.

From Middle Dutch stric, stricke, strec, from Old Dutch stric, from Proto-Germanic *strikkiz (“line; rope”), from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“stiff; rigid; tight; rope; cord”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter- (“stiff”).

From Middle Dutch struuf, from Old Dutch *strūf, from Proto-Germanic *strūbaz (“stiff, rough, bristly, shaggy”), from Proto-Indo-European *strewbʰ-, *strewb- (“stiff”). Cognate with Middle Low German struuf, West Frisian stroef, German straub and struppig.
From Middle Dutch stronc, from Old Dutch strunc, from Proto-Germanic *strunkaz. Cognate with German Strunk (“hard stalk, as in cabbage, etc.”).
From Middle Dutch stropen, from Proto-Germanic *straupijaną, causative of Proto-Germanic *streupaną.
From Middle Dutch struuc, from Proto-Germanic *strūka, according to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *streug-, *streuk-, extended from *ster- (“stiff”).
From Middle Dutch tachtich, from Old Dutch *antahtoda, *ahtodig, *antahtodig, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutēhundą.

parole.significato: teal, one of certain small ducks of the genera Anas and Spatula
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch talinc, from Proto-Germanic *tailijaz, of unknown ultimate origin, with no cognates outside of Germanic. English teal is a cognate.

From Middle Dutch tas, tasse, from Old Dutch *tas, *tasso, compare Old English tas and English tass (from Frankish), from Proto-Germanic *tassaz (“pile, heap”), Proto-Indo-European *dāy- (“to divide, split, section, part, separate”).
From Middle Dutch te, from Old Dutch te, ti, from Proto-Germanic *ta.

parole.significato: Created verbs with a sense of ‘in pieces, apart, asunder’, or with intensive force.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch te-, from Old Dutch te-, from Proto-Germanic *twiz-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwis-. Compare German zer-.

From Middle Dutch teder, teeder, from Old Dutch *tidar, from Proto-Germanic *tidaraz, of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps from the same source as *taitaz (“delicate, tender”). Cognate with German Low German teder (“fine; delicate; thin; sensitive; tender; weak”). Compare also West Frisian tear
From Middle Dutch teer, contraction of teder, teeder, from Old Dutch *tidar, from Proto-Germanic *tidaraz. Doublet of teder. Cognate to Middle English teere.
From Middle Dutch têkenen, from Old Dutch *tēkanen, from Proto-Germanic *taiknijaną. Equivalent to teken (“sign, signal”) + -en.

From Middle Dutch toghel, teugel, from Proto-Germanic *tugilaz (“rein on a horse”), whence also Old Norse tygill, Old English tigel, Old High German zugil (German Zügel). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-. Equivalent to tijgen + -el.
From Middle Dutch tiende, from Old Dutch *tiando, from Proto-Germanic *tehundô.

Uncertain. Possibly deverbal from tillen (“to lift up”); some early attestations of the word refer specifically to the hatch used to close off a dovecote. The meaning "dovecote" then originates as a pars pro toto usage. An alternative possibility is that the word represents a Frisian form correspond
From Middle Dutch tin, ten, from Old Dutch *tin, from Proto-Germanic *tiną.
From Middle Dutch tinne, from Proto-Germanic *tindijō (“point, peak, pinnacle”) or *tinnō, *tinnǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts (“tooth”).
From Middle Dutch tip, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tuppijô, *tuppijǭ (“tip”), a diminutive of *tuppaz.
From Middle Dutch tocht or tucht, from Old Dutch *tuht, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tuhtiz, cognate to German Zucht. Equivalent to tijgen (“to go, pull”) + -t (“verbal noun”). Doublet of tucht.

parole.significato: to remain somewhere; to linger, stay
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch toeven, from Old Dutch *tuoven, from Proto-Germanic *tōbijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *debʰ-, see also Sanskrit दिप्सति (dipsati, “to deceive”). Cognate with Low German töven, Swedish töva.

From Middle Dutch tônen, from Old Dutch *tōnen. Cognate with Middle Low German tônen, Middle High German zounen, zōnen. Probably a byform of synonymous Middle Dutch tôghen, cognate with Old Saxon tōgian, Old High German zougen, Gothic 𐌰𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ataugjan), derived from Proto-Germanic *augô (“eye”). T
From Old Dutch *tōien, variant of *touwen (from which touwen), from Proto-Germanic *tawjaną.
From Middle Dutch torn, from Old Dutch *torn, from Proto-Germanic *turnaz. Cognate with German Zorn. Attested since 1240.

First attested in the early sixteenth century and thus not attested in Middle Dutch and Old Dutch, but ultimately inherited from Proto-Germanic *taltrōną; compare Old English tealtrian. The shift from -alt- to -out- is the result of Middle Dutch L-vocalization.
From Middle Dutch troost, from Old Dutch trōst, from Proto-Germanic *traustą.
From Middle Dutch trôosten, from Old Dutch trōsten, from Proto-Germanic *traustijaną. Cognate with German trösten.
From Middle Dutch trouwen, from Old Dutch *triuwon, from Proto-Germanic *trewwāną. Equivalent to trouw (“loyality”) + -en or trouw (“faithful, loyal”) + -en.

parole.significato: discipline, a regime entailing strict supervision and/or punishment
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tucht, tocht, from Old Dutch *tuht, from Proto-Germanic *tuhtiz. Equivalent to tijgen (“to go, pull”) + -t (“verbal noun”). Doublet of tocht. Compare also German Zucht.
From Middle Dutch tumelen, a frequentative derived from tumen, from Old Dutch *tūmon, from Proto-Germanic *tūmōną (“to turn, rotate”).

From Middle Dutch twisschen, tusschen, a shortening of Old Dutch intwiskan, originally a prepositional phrase *in twiskan. The latter word is from Proto-Germanic *twiskaz, *twiskijaz (“twofold, double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, doubly; in two”).

From Middle Dutch twalef, twaelf (also twelef, tweelf), from Old Dutch *twalif, *twelif, from Proto-Germanic *twalif. The reason for the lack of umlaut in the form with a is unknown. It may be that the position between /w/ and (velarized) /l/ hindered umlaut in some dialects. Cognate with German zwö

parole.significato: a pair of twins; said of people and other mammals
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch twiling, twilling, tweiling, from Old Dutch *twinling, possibly from Proto-Germanic *twinilingaz, with the first element from *twinaz (compare German Zwilling, English twinling, Danish tvilling). By surface analysis, twee (“two”) + -ling.
From Middle Dutch twijch, from Old Dutch *twīg, from Proto-Germanic *twīgaz (“branch, twig”). Related to twee.
From Middle Dutch twintich, from Old Dutch *twēntig, from Proto-Germanic *twai tigiwiz.

From Proto-Germanic *twistaz (“strife, quarrel”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Twist (“discord”), German Low German Twist (“strife; discord”), German Zwist (“turmoil; strife; discord”), Swedish tvist (“quarrel; dispute”), Icelandic tvistur (“deuce”), and English twist.
From Middle Dutch uider, ûder, from Old Dutch *ūdar, from Proto-Germanic *ūdarą (“udder”). Cognate with English udder. Doublet of jadder.
From Middle Dutch ūtgang, from Old Dutch *ūtgang, from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz. Cognate with German Ausgang, English outgang.

parole.significato: vane, small flag (often pointed or pronged)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vāne, from Old Dutch *fano, from Proto-Germanic *fanô.

From Middle Dutch vacht, from Old Dutch *faht, from Proto-Germanic *fahtiz, from Proto-Indo-European *póḱtis, from the root *peḱ-. Related to Old Dutch fas (“head hair”) and Middle Dutch vas (“head hair”). Cognate with Old English feht.
From Middle Dutch vaderlik, from Old Dutch *fadarlīk, from Proto-Germanic *fadurlīkaz, equivalent to vader + -lijk. Cognate with English fatherly, German väterlich.

Alteration of earlier van haver tot haver kennen, which in turn represents a folk-etymological alteration of Middle Dutch van aver te avere, meaning "from descendant to descendant" (i.e. "from father to son"; see Proto-Germanic *aferô), a form which seems to have survived dialectally into Modern Dut

From Middle Dutch vanden, from Old Dutch *fandon, from Proto-Germanic *fandōną (“to seek, to search for, to examine”), an o-grade iterative derived from *finþaną (“to find”) (modern vinden). Cognate to English fand (“to search; to try; to examine”), German fahnden (“(law enforcement) to search”).
From Middle Dutch varre, verre, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *farzô (“bull, ox”). Related to vaars (“heifer”).

From Middle Dutch varken, verken, from Old Dutch farkīn, ferkīn, an old diminutive, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *farhaz (Proto-West Germanic *farh) + Proto-Germanic *-ukaz (Proto-Germanic *-ukīn, with another diminutive suffix attached). Compare Central Franconian Ferke, Low German Farken.

parole.significato: fast (period of time when one abstains from or eats very little food)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vastene f, from Old Dutch *fastunna, from Proto-Germanic *fastubniją, *fastubnijō, from *fastāną (“to fast”). Cognate with Old Saxon fastunnia, Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌿𐌱𐌽𐌹 (fastubni).
From Middle Dutch veechte (“enmity”), from *(ge)veech, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *faihaz. Related to English foe.
From Middle Dutch vele, from Old Dutch filo, from Proto-Germanic *felu.
From Middle Dutch viertien, veertien, from Old Dutch *viurtēn, *viurtien, *fiortian, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun. Compare German vierzehn, West Frisian fjirtjin, English fourteen, Danish fjorten.
From Middle Dutch viertich, vēertich, from Old Dutch *viertig, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr tigiwiz.

From Middle Dutch veest, from vijst, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *fistaz (“breaking wind, fart”). Cognate to English fist (“fart”) and English fise, and more distantly German Furz through a Proto-Indo-European variant of the same root.
From Middle Dutch veilen, from the adjective veile (“for sale”), ultimately from a form related to Proto-Germanic *falaz (“for sale”).
From Middle Dutch vēlen, from Old Dutch *felan, from Proto-Germanic *felhaną.
From Middle Dutch velge, from Old Dutch *felga, from Proto-Germanic *felgō.

parole.significato: mere, a small shallow lake or pond
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch venne, from Old Dutch *feni, from Proto-Germanic *fanją (compare English fen). Doublet of veen.
From Middle Dutch verbot, from Old Dutch *verbot, from Proto-Germanic *furibudą. Compare German Verbot, Swedish förbud, Danish forbud, English forbid.
From Proto-Germanic *fradailijaną, equivalent to ver- + delen. Cognate with German verteilen, Old English fordǣlan.
From Middle Dutch verdoemen, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *fradōmijaną, equivalent to doem + ver- -en.
From Middle Dutch verdrāgen, from Old Dutch *fardragan, from Proto-Germanic *fradraganą. Equivalent to ver- + dragen.
From Middle Dutch verdwinen, from ver- + dwinen. Compare Old English fordwīnan. The base verb derives from Old Dutch *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną.
From Middle Dutch veren, from Old Dutch ferien, from Proto-Germanic *farjaną.

parole.significato: to pay back, to punish, to retaliate
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vergelden, from Old Dutch fargeldan, from Proto-Germanic *frageldaną. Equivalent to ver- + gelden.
From Middle Dutch vergen, from Old Dutch *fergon, from Proto-Germanic *fergōną. Cognate with Old Saxon fergon, West Frisian fergje, German fergen, Old Norse fergja.
From Middle Dutch vergēven, from Old Dutch *fargevan, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną.
From Proto-Germanic *frahelaną, equivalent to ver- + helen.

From Middle Dutch verliesen, from Old Dutch farliesan, from Proto-Germanic *fraleusaną. Cognate with German verlieren. Compare Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “loose, untie”), Latin solvō (“dissolve”), English forlorn.

parole.significato: to make famous, to make one's accomplishments known
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vermaren, from Old Dutch *firmāren, from Proto-Germanic *mērijaną. Corresponds to ver- + maren.

parole.significato: to learn (of), to find out, to hear (about)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vernēmen, from Old Dutch farneman, from Proto-Germanic *franemaną. Equivalent to ver- + nemen.

From Middle Dutch vernielen, a verb derived (with the circumfix ver- -en) from the word niel, which appears to have meant "prone", and which derives from Proto-Germanic *nīwalaz (compare Old English neowol). The verb thus originally may have meant "to topple" or "to overthrow".
From Middle Dutch vervāren, from Old Dutch farfaran, from Proto-Germanic *frafaraną. Equivalent to ver- + varen.
From Middle Dutch verwerden, from Old Dutch *farwerthan, from Proto-Germanic *frawerþaną (“to perish, come to ruin”), equivalent to ver- + worden. Cognate with English forworth.
From Middle Dutch versene, from Old Dutch *fersana, from Proto-Germanic *fersnō, from Proto-Indo-European *tpḗrsneh₂.

parole.significato: to fix, to fasten, to attach
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vesten, from Old Dutch festen, from Proto-Germanic *fastijaną, from *fastuz (modern vast).
From Middle Dutch veter, from Old Dutch *fetera, from Proto-Germanic *feterō. Cognate with English fetter.

parole.significato: a foal, the young of any equine and some other quadrupeds, either colt (male) or filly (female); unless specified, usua…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch volen, from Old Dutch *folīn, from Proto-Germanic *fulīną, from *fulô, cognate with English foal, German Fohlen.
From Middle Dutch vijfte, from Old Dutch *fīfto, from Proto-Germanic *fimftô.
From Middle Dutch vijftien, from Old Dutch *vīftēn, *vīftien, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun. Compare West Frisian fyftjin, German fünfzehn, English fifteen, Danish femten.
From Middle Dutch vijftich, from Old Dutch *fīftig, from Proto-Germanic *fimf tigiwiz.

Folk-etymological alteration of an unattested western form (with regular shift of -alt- to -out-; compare woud) of the attested Middle Dutch vīvalter (an eastern form, as evidenced by the lack of the aforementioned shift to -out-), from Old Dutch *fifaltra, from Proto-Germanic *fifaldǭ. Germanic cog
From Middle Dutch vinne, from Old Dutch *finna, from Proto-Germanic *finnō.

parole.significato: a fisher, a fisherman or, less commonly, a fisherwoman
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vischer, visscher, from Old Dutch *fiskar, from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz. Equivalent to vissen + -er.
From Middle Dutch vlage, from Proto-Germanic *flagōn-, which could be related to *fleuganą (“to fly”), or otherwise to the root of Old English flacor (“flying, flickering”).
From Middle Dutch vlas, from Old Dutch *flas, from earlier *flahs, from Proto-Germanic *flahsą, from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to fold, plait, weave”); thus distantly related to vlechten.
From Middle Dutch vlechten, from Old Dutch *flehtan, from Proto-Germanic *flehtaną.
From Middle Dutch vloghel, vlueghel, from Old Dutch *flugil, from Proto-Germanic *flugilaz. Equivalent to vliegen + -el.

From Middle Dutch vlien, from Old Dutch *flion, from Proto-Germanic *fleuhaną. The -d- originates as a hypercorrection probably based on a mistaken assumption of d-weakening (a phenomenon observed in Dutch in words such leder / leer). A similar case of hypercorrection can be found in bevrijden, whic
From Middle Dutch vloer, from Old Dutch *fluor, from Proto-Germanic *flōraz.

From Middle Dutch vlote, from Proto-Germanic *flutô (“floating object”) an ablauted noun derived from the stem of vlieten. Cognate to Old Saxon flota, Middle Low German vlote, Old High German flozza, German Flosse, West Frisian float, Old English flota, Old Norse floti.

From Middle Dutch vlot, ultimately from a conflation of Proto-Germanic *flutą (“flow; stream”) and Proto-Germanic *flutô (“small boat”). Cognate with West Frisian flot (“raft”), German Low German Flott, Flött (“raft”), Old English flot (“sea”), Old English flota (“ship; vessel; fleet”), Old Norse fl
From vol- + tooien, a by-form of obsolete touwen (compare getouw) ultimately deriving from Proto-Germanic *tawjaną.

parole.significato: spark (a small particle of glowing matter, either molten material or from fire)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vonke, from Old Dutch funko, from Proto-Germanic *funkô. Cognate with Old High German funko, funcho (German Funke), English funk (“spark, touchwood”).
From older voye, from Old Dutch fōa, from Proto-Germanic *fuhǭ.
From Middle Dutch vort, voort, from Old Dutch forth, from Proto-Germanic *furþą, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥to-. Compare English forth.

From Middle Dutch voorwaerde, from vore + waerde, the latter from Old Dutch *warda, from Proto-Germanic *wardō. Cognate with Middle High German vorwort (“provision, treaty”), Middle English forward, forword (“agreement, covenant”).
From Proto-Germanic *fausaz (“rotten”).

parole.significato: to progress, advance, to bring forward
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vorderen, from Old Dutch fortheron, from Proto-Germanic *furþerōną.

From Middle Dutch vorsch, from Old Dutch *frosk, from Proto-Germanic *fruskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *prew- (“jump, hop”). Cognate with German Frosch, West Frisian froask, dialectal English frosh, Icelandic froskur.
From Middle Dutch vreden, from Old Dutch *frithon, from Proto-Germanic *friþōną.
From Middle Dutch vrêse, from Old Dutch frēsa, from Proto-Germanic *fraisō (“danger”).
From Middle Dutch vreuchde, from Proto-Germanic *frawiþō, from *frawaz (“glad”) + *-iþō.
From Middle Dutch vrêsen, from Old Dutch *frēson, from Proto-Germanic *fraisōną.
From Middle Dutch vrintlec, vriendelijc, from Old Dutch *friuntlik, *friuntlik, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndlīkaz. By surface analysis, vriend + -lijk. Cognate to German freundlich, English friendly.

From Middle Dutch vroet, vroot, from Old Dutch *fruot, from Proto-Germanic *frōdaz. Cognate with English frood from Old English frōd (“wise, knowing”), Old Saxon frōd, Old Frisian frōd, Old High German fruot, Old Norse fróðr, Icelandic fróður, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐍉𐌸𐍃 (frōþs).
From Middle Dutch vroeden, from Old Dutch *fruoden, from Proto-Germanic *frōdijaną.
From Middle Dutch vrôlijc, from Old Dutch frōlīk, from *frō + -līk, the former part from Proto-Germanic *frawaz, the latter from *-līkaz.
From Middle Dutch vrōme (“firm, upright”), an adjective derived from the noun vrōme (“benefit, use”), from Old Dutch *fruma, from Proto-Germanic *frumô.

parole.significato: fishing water subject to manorial tenure
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vrône, from Old Dutch frōno, from Proto-Germanic *frawjô.
From Middle Dutch vruchte, from Old Dutch forhta. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *furhtį̄ (“fear”), from Proto-Indo-European *perg- (“to frighten; fear”).

parole.significato: made of the wood of the Norway spruce
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vurin, from Old Dutch *furīn, from Proto-Germanic *furhīnaz, from *furhō.
From Middle Dutch wāre, from Old Dutch *wara, from Proto-Germanic *warō, probably related to *waraz (“wary, watchful”). Cognate with English ware.
From Middle Dutch wāert, wēert, from Old Dutch *wert, from Proto-Germanic *werduz.
From Middle Dutch wert, wāert, from Old Dutch werth, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz.
From Middle Dutch wāernen, from Old Dutch *warnon, from Proto-Germanic *warnōną.

parole.significato: the function, duty of standing guard; a watch or vigil
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wachte, from Old Dutch wahta, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.
From Middle Dutch wade, from Old Dutch *watho, from Proto-Germanic *waþwô. Cognate with German Wade (“calf (of leg)”), Swedish vad (“calf (of leg)”) and Afrikaans waai (“popliteal”).

From Middle Dutch wade, reformed from waet through influence of the collective gewade (modern gewaad). Further from Old Dutch *wāt, from Proto-Germanic *wēd-. Cognate with Middle High German wāt, Old Saxon wād, Old English wǣd, Old Norse váð.
From Middle Dutch wāden, from Old Dutch *wadan, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną.

Inherited from Middle Dutch wafel, wafele, wavel, from Old Dutch *wāvila, from Proto-Germanic *wēbilǭ, *wēbilō, possibly related to Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to braid, weave”) (whence Dutch weven (“to weave”) and English weave).

parole.significato: a wake (a gathering to remember a dead person)
parole.testo: From Old Dutch *waka, from Proto-Germanic *wakō, related to the verb *wakjaną.
From Old Dutch walm (“heat, glow, zeal”), from Proto-Germanic *wallaną (“to spring, well, bubble”). Compare Old English wilm (“cooking, boiling, undulating movement”).
From Middle Dutch walnote, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *walhahnuts (“foreign nut; walnut”). Compare English walnut.

From Middle Dutch wamme, wam (“belly; stomach”), from Old Dutch wamba (“belly; body”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“belly, stomach, abdomen”), from Proto-Indo-European *wamp- (“membrane (of bowels), intestines, womb”). Related to Dutch wambuis (“gambeson”), from wamb (“belly”) + buis (“ja

parole.significato: bad, un- (preceding nouns, verbs and adjectives)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wan-, from Old Dutch *wan-, from Proto-Germanic *wana-, a prefixing form of *wanaz.
From Middle Dutch want, from Proto-Germanic *wanduz (“wickerwork; barrier, fence”). Cognate with German Wand.
From Middle Dutch want, from Old Dutch wanda, from Proto-Germanic *hwandê. Cognate with Old High German wanta, Middle High German wante.

parole.significato: a coarse type of woolen fabric; anything made from it
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch want, gewant, from Old Dutch *giwant, from Proto-Germanic *gawandą, from the root of winden.
From Middle Dutch was, from Old Dutch was, from Proto-Germanic *wahsą. Cognate with German Wachs, English wax, Danish voks, Swedish vax.

parole.significato: to water, to irrigate, to soak
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wateren, weteren, from Old Dutch *wateron, *weteren, from Proto-Germanic *watrōną, *watrijaną. Equivalent to water + -en.
From Middle Dutch webbe, from Old Dutch *web, from Proto-Germanic *wabją, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“weave”).

From Middle Dutch wedde, from a byform of Proto-Germanic *wadą, whence wad. Closely related with Middle High German wete, wettin f (“drinking place, shallow pond”). The Dutch appears to require a neuter *wadją (though feminine use is also attested), the High German a feminine īn-stem *wadį̄.

parole.significato: twig, especially of an oak or willow
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wēde, from Old Dutch *widu, from Proto-Germanic *widuz.
From Middle Dutch weiden, from Old Dutch *weithon, from Proto-Germanic *waiþoną, *waiþijaną. Equivalent to weide + -en.

parole.significato: little, few, not much, not many
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch weinich, wenich, from Old Dutch *weinag, *wēnag, from Proto-Germanic *wainagaz. Cognate with German wenig (“few”).

parole.significato: the opposite of not (used to add positive emphasis to the verb, much like the auxiliaries do or does in affirmative sen…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wel, from Old Dutch *wela, wala, from Proto-Germanic *wela, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. Compare German wohl, English well, Icelandic vel, Swedish väl, Danish and Norwegian vel.
From Middle Dutch weldaet, from Old Dutch weladāt, from Proto-Germanic *weladēdiz. Equivalent to wel- + daad.
From Middle Dutch welc, from Old Dutch *wilik, *welik, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wiljakumô. Cognate to English welcome, West Frisian wolkom, German willkommen, Danish velkommen and Norwegian Bokmål velkommen.

parole.significato: whelp, young mammal of certain carnivorous species, notably a canine pup, bear cub or lion cub
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch welp, from Old Dutch welp, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz.

parole.significato: to bend like an arch, to arch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch welven, a mixture of two Old Dutch [Term?] verbs: * *welvan, from Proto-Germanic *hwelbaną, a class 3 strong verb. * *welven, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbijaną, a class 1 weak verb.
From Proto-Germanic *hwannē. Cognate with English when, German wenn, Low German wenn.
From Middle Dutch wênen, from Old Dutch wēnon, from Proto-Germanic *wainōną. Cognate to German weinen.

From Middle Dutch wintbrauwe, from Old Dutch *wintbrāwa. The first element (Old Dutch *wint) is unknown but presumed to be related to Ancient Greek ἴονθος (íonthos). The second element (Old Dutch *brāwa) is from Proto-Germanic *brēwō. Wenkbrauw is a doublet of wimper (“eyelash”), from a contraction.
From Middle Dutch wenken, from Old Dutch *wenken, from Proto-Germanic *wankijaną.
From Middle Dutch wenschen, also wonschen, wunschen in the eastern dialects, from Old Dutch *wunsken, from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną.
From Middle Dutch wervel, from Old Dutch *wirvil, from Proto-Germanic *hwirbilaz.

From Middle Dutch wichelen, wigelen, wijchelen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wigulōną, *wihulōną (“to conjure, divine”). Related to Old English wiglian. Originally a frequentative verb (suffixed with -elen) related to wikken, which is derived from Proto-Germanic *wikkōną. More at witch.
From Middle Dutch wicht, from Old Dutch *wiht, from Proto-Germanic *wihtą. Cognate with English wight, German Wicht.
From Middle Dutch wijt, from Old Dutch wīdo, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz. Compare Low German wied, West Frisian wiid, German weit, English wide, Danish vid.

From Middle Dutch wīde, from Old Dutch *wīda (in toponyms), from Proto-Germanic *wīþijō (“willow”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis (“that which twines or bends, branch, switch”). Cognate with German Weide.
From Middle Dutch wijs, from Old Dutch wīs, from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz.
From Old Dutch *wīsa, from Proto-Germanic *wīsǭ (“manner, way”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”), related to Etymology 1.

From Middle Dutch wimbrauw, contraction of wintbrauwe, from Old Dutch *wintbrāwa. The first element is unknown but presumed to be related to Ancient Greek ἴονθος (íonthos); the second element is from Proto-Germanic *brēwō. Doublet of wenkbrauw (“eyebrow”). The form wimper is native in some Dutch dia

parole.significato: to wind (turn coils of something around)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch winden, from Old Dutch *windan, from Proto-Germanic *windaną.
From Middle Dutch winter, from Old Dutch winter, from Proto-Germanic *wintruz.
Derived from Proto-Germanic *wissaz, past participle of *witaną.

parole.significato: cubic metre (mainly when used for firewood)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wisse, from Old Dutch *withtha, from Proto-Germanic *wiþjǭ. The development *-þj- > -ss- is also found in smidse (from earlier smisse); original *-þþ- becomes -tt- in lat, mot.

parole.significato: points; switch (in Flanders a "wissel" has the normal masculine grammatical gender, in the railroad sector in the Nethe…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wissel, from Old Dutch *wissel, from Proto-Germanic *wihslaz.
From Middle Dutch wisselen, from Old Dutch *wissalon, from Proto-Germanic *wihslōną. Equivalent to wissel + -en.
From Middle Dutch wisschen, from Old Dutch *wisken, from Proto-Germanic *wiskijaną.
From Middle Dutch woet, from Old Dutch *wuot, *wuodi, from Proto-Germanic *wōþuz. Compare English wode.
From Middle Dutch woeker, from Old Dutch *wuokar, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz. Compare German Wucher, English oker.
From Middle Dutch wonde, wunde, from Old Dutch wunda, from Proto-Germanic *wundō. Compare Low German Wunn, German Wunde, West Frisian wûne, English wound, Icelandic und.

parole.significato: worm, vernacular term for various, mostly legless invertebrates; often nematodes or legless arthropod larvae.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch worm, from Old Dutch *wurm, *worm, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis. Compare English worm, West Frisian wjirm, German Wurm, Danish orm.

From Middle Dutch wortele, from Old Dutch *wurtala, from Proto-Germanic *wurt- (“root”) + *waluz (“stick”), formed from the Proto-Indo-European roots *wréh₂ds + *welH-. Unknown. Possibly from Middle Dutch waut, wout (“authority, power”), from Proto-Germanic *waldą. Related with Dutch geweld (“violence”). parole.significato: wart (type of growth occurring on the skin)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wratte, from Old Dutch wratt, *wratta, *warta, from Proto-Germanic *wartǭ. The phonetic development is irregular, but compare Middle Low German wratte, Middle English wrette. Some modern Dutch dialects have the expected form wa(a)rt. Compare also German Warze, English wart.

With final -f influenced by wrijven (“to rub”), from dialectal wreeg, from Middle Dutch *wrēghe, unattested variant of wrijghe, wrijch (“instep”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrīhan-. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrigōną (“to wriggle”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyḱ- (“to turn, wrap, tie”), from *wer- (“to turn, bend”). Perhaps related to Low German wriggen (“to twist”).
From Middle Dutch wringen, from Old Dutch *wringan, from Proto-Germanic *wringaną.
From Middle Dutch wroegen, from Old Dutch *wruogen, from Proto-Germanic *wrōgijaną.

parole.significato: the common curlew, Eurasian curlew (Numenius arquata)
parole.testo: Perhaps ultimately from a Proto-Germanic *hwelpaną (“to cry, yelp”), whence *hwelpaz (“whelp”) may also derive. Alternatively, from the same root as *hwelbaną (“to curve”) (Dutch welven), referring to the curved beak characteristic of curlews. Cognates include Saterland Frisian Wilp, West Frisian wy
From Middle Dutch worgen, wurgen, from Old Dutch *wurgen, from Proto-Germanic *wurgijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”). Cognate with German würgen, English worry.

parole.significato: saddle (seat on a horse or a bicycle)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sādel, from Old Dutch *sadul, *sadal, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz.

parole.significato: to fall, to drop, to sink
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *sacken, from Old Dutch *sackon, from Proto-Germanic *sakkōną, further etymology unknown, perhaps from a denasalized derivative of *sinkwaną (“to sink”); compare English sag. According to Kluge, related to zak (“sack”). Found natively only in the West Germanic languages.

parole.significato: a norms or habit practiced by a certain people that is considered to be just and desirable by them
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sēde, from Old Dutch sido, from Proto-Germanic *siduz. Compare German Sitte.

parole.significato: seal, any member of the family Phocidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch seehont. By surface analysis, zee (“sea”) + hond (“hound, dog”). Middle Dutch seehont, is possibly an alteration of seelhont (literally “seal-hound, seal-dog”), from seel (“seal”), from Proto-Germanic *selhaz. Compare Low German Saalhund (“seal”).
From Middle Dutch sêem, from Old Dutch sēm, from Proto-Germanic *saimaz.
From Middle Dutch sêer, from Old Dutch sēr, from Proto-Germanic *sairaz.
From Middle Dutch sêer, from Old Dutch sēr, from Proto-Germanic *sairą.

parole.significato: very, to a high degree or intensity
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sêre, from Old Dutch sēro, from Proto-Germanic *sairaz. Equivalent to adverbial use of etymology 1.

From Middle Dutch selsiene, selsane, selsene, also selsame, from Old Dutch *seldsiuni, *seldsāni, from Proto-Germanic *seldasiuniz (“rarely seen”), a compound of *seldaz (“rare”) + *siuniz (“sight”). The formation with -zaam is by analogy and occurred in Middle Dutch because the original formation o

parole.significato: oneself, referring to the subject of a sentence: myself, yourself, itself, ourselves, themselves etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch self, from Old Dutch self, *selvo, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”), from *s(w)e- (“separate, apart”). Compare Low German sulv, West Frisian self, English self, German selbst, selber, Danish selv.
From Middle Dutch senewe, senuw, from Old Dutch *senawa, from Proto-Germanic *senawō. Cognate with English sinew.
From Middle Dutch seste, from Old Dutch *sesto, from Proto-Germanic *sehstô.
From Middle Dutch sestien, from Old Dutch *sestēn, *sestien, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun. Compare West Frisian sechstjin, German sechzehn, English sixteen, Danish seksten.
From Middle Dutch sestich, also tsestich with t- from tsēventich, from Old Dutch *sestig, from Proto-Germanic *sehs tigiwiz.

parole.significato: chair, seat, especially as in parliament
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch setel, from Old Dutch *setal, *setl, from Proto-Germanic *setlaz. More at settee and settle.
From Middle Dutch sēvende, from Old Dutch *sivondo, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô.
From Middle Dutch seventien, from Old Dutch *sivontēn, *sivontien, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Compare English seventeen, West Frisian santjin, German siebzehn, Danish sytten.
From Middle Dutch sēventich, from Old Dutch *sivontig, but also Middle Dutch tsēventich, from Old Dutch *antsivontig, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą.

parole.significato: she; third-person singular feminine subjective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sī, from Old Dutch siu, sia, from Proto-Germanic *iz and *hiz.
From Middle Dutch zijt, sijt (“wide, broad”), from Old Dutch *sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīdaz (“ample”).
From Middle Dutch sipen, from Old Dutch *sīpan, from Proto-Germanic *sīpaną.
From Middle Dutch silver, from Old Dutch silver, from Proto-Germanic *silubrą.
From Middle Dutch silveren, from Old Dutch *silverin, from Proto-Germanic *silubrīnaz, equivalent to zilver + -en.
From Middle Dutch singen, from Old Dutch singan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-.
From Middle Dutch sode, from Old Dutch *sōtho, from Proto-Germanic *sauþô. Related to Middle Low German sode, English sod.

Univerbation of zo (“so”) + dra (“soon”), the latter from Middle Dutch drâde; compare weldra (“soon”). Likely related to Dutch draaien (“to turn”), with an unclear development of sense, in which case from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną. In this case cognate with German drehen (“to throw”) and English throw.

From Middle Dutch zoene, soen, soene, swoene (“reconciliation; atonement; kiss”), from Old Dutch *sōna, *swōna (“reconciliation; peace; agreement”), from Proto-Germanic *sōnō, *swōnō (“appeasement; reconciliation; atonement; sacrifice”), from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vig
From Middle Dutch soet, from Proto-Germanic *sōtą.
From Middle Dutch sōmer, from Old Dutch sumar, from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz.

parole.significato: a long narrow inlet, or a strait between the mainland and an island; a sound
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sunt, from Old Dutch *sunt, from Proto-Germanic *sundą. Cognate to English sound, Danish sund (“sound; strait; channel”), Swedish sund (“sound; strait; channel”), Icelandic sund (“sound; strait; channel”). Related to zwemmen. Not related to zondvloed.

parole.significato: sin (offence against moral and/or divine law)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sonde, from Old Dutch sunda, from Proto-Germanic *sundijō.
From Middle Dutch sonder, from Old Dutch sundar, from Proto-Germanic *sundraz. Cognate with English sunder.
From Middle Dutch sonderen, from Old Dutch *sundron, from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną.
From earlier zode, from Middle Dutch sôde (“something boiled”), from Old Dutch *sōtho, from Proto-Germanic *sauþô, from the same root as zieden (“to boil”). Cognate with Sod- in German Sodbrennen.
From Middle Dutch sôor, from Old Dutch *sōr, Proto-Germanic *sauzaz (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂sows- (“dry, parched”). Cognate with English sear.

From Middle Dutch souten, from Old Dutch *saltan, from Proto-Germanic *saltaną. The verb was originally a class 7 strong verb, but the verb became weak early on and only the strong past participle was preserved. The past form would have been *zielt, parallel to houden and hield.

From Middle Dutch suder, from Old Dutch *sūthar, from Proto-Germanic *sunþra-. In Middle Dutch, the word was still used on its own; by Modern Dutch times, the word has turned into a prefix not encountered as an adjective proper outside compounds. Nonetheless, spellings where zuider was separated fro

parole.significato: to swig, to drink heavily, to guzzle
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch supen, from Old Dutch *sūpan, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną.
From Middle Dutch sulc, solc, selc, swelc, swilc, from Old Dutch sulich, *sulik, from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz.

parole.significato: a horizontal structural member of a building near ground level bearing the upright portion of a frame, like for a door…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sille, sulle, from Old Dutch *sulla, from Proto-Germanic *sulī (“balk”). Cognate to English sill.

From Middle Dutch sulte (“brine, salted food”), from Old Dutch sulta (“salt water”), from Proto-Germanic *sultijō (“salt water, brine”). Cognate with Old Saxon sultia, Old High German sulza (German Sülze).
From Middle Dutch suur, from Old Dutch *sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūrą, related to Etymology 1 above.

parole.significato: a swan, a large waterbird of the genera Cygnus and Coscoroba
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch swane, from Old Dutch *swano, from Proto-Germanic *swanô. Existed next to Middle Dutch swan, from Old Dutch *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz. Cognate with Low German Swaan, West Frisian swan, German Schwan, English swan, Swedish svan.
From Middle Dutch swam, from Old Dutch *swam, from Proto-Germanic *swammaz. Cognate with German Schwamm (“sponge”).
From Middle Dutch swēvel, swāvel, from Old Dutch *sweval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz.

parole.significato: a purulent boil, skin injury containing pus, ulcer
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch swēre, from Old Dutch swero (“boil, abscess”), from Proto-Germanic *swerô (“ulcer”), from *sweraną (“to hurt; fester”).

From Middle Dutch sweet, swet, from Old Dutch *sweit, *swēt, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd-, *sweyd-. Compare German Schweiß, West Frisian swit, English sweat, Danish sved.

parole.significato: to eat greedily, gulp down, gobble up, guzzle
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch swelgen, from Old Dutch *swelgan, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą.
From Middle Dutch swellen, from Old Dutch *swellan, from Proto-Germanic *swellaną.

From Middle Dutch swepen, from Old Dutch *swipon, *swipen, from Proto-Germanic *swipjaną (“to move”) and Proto-Germanic *swipǭ (“whip, lash”). Cognate with West Frisian swypkje (“to whip”), Middle English swippen (“to strike, move swiftly, glide”).
From Middle Dutch swēren, from Old Dutch *sweran, from Proto-Germanic *sweraną.
From Middle Dutch swarm, swerm, swaerm, from Old Dutch *swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”). Compare German Schwarm, English swarm, Danish sværm.
From Middle Dutch swerven, from Old Dutch *swervan, from Proto-Germanic *swerbaną.
From Middle Dutch swēven, from Old Dutch sweven, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną.
From zwezer (“thymus; testicle”), of unclear origin; perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *swēsaz. For the suffix, compare wederik, dravik.
From Middle Dutch swichten. Ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *swībaną.
From Middle Dutch swijm, related to Middle High German swīm (modern German Schweim), Middle Low German swîm. Likely a strengthening of the weak Old Dutch *swīmo, from Proto-Germanic *swīmô.
From Middle Dutch zwikken, from Old Dutch *swikkon, from Proto-Germanic *swikkōną an iterative to Proto-Germanic *swīkwaną (“to move out of the way”), whence Dutch zwijken.

From zwoord, a dialectal form of early modern Dutch zwaert, zweerd, from Middle Dutch swaerde (“hairy skin”), from Old Dutch *swarda, from Proto-Germanic *swardō (“overgrown surface”). From Middle Dutch almechtich, from Old Dutch *alamahtīg (debatably attested in the Old Saxon Baptismal Vow, the linguistic classification of which is unclear and which contains Old Dutch features), from Proto-Germanic *alamahtīgaz. From Middle Dutch gelde, probably borrowed from Old Norse geldr (“barren, yielding no milk”), from Proto-Germanic *galdaz, *galdijaz (“barren, unfruitful”). The ultimate origin is uncertain; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to cut”), or from *gʰel- (“to shout, cry”).

parole.significato: millet (any of a group of various types of grass or its grains used as food)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch heerse, from Proto-Germanic *hirsijô, potentially derived in turn from an unknown substrate language or, alternatively, from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“feed, nourish”). Cognate with Limburgish hirs, Old Saxon hirsi, Plautdietsch Hieezh, Old High German hirsi (German Hirse), Aleman
From Middle Dutch hanteren, hantieren, from Old French hanter, via Old Norse (or possibly Old English) from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną.

From Middle Dutch heugen, huegen, hogen, from Old Dutch *hugon, from Proto-West Germanic *hugōn, from Proto-Germanic *hugōną (“to think, consider”). parole.significato: uvula (appendage that hangs from the palate)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch huch, huuch, huych, borrowed through Middle High German from Middle Low German hûk. Of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly borrowed from North Germanic, or possibly from a variant of Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ (“head covering”).

parole.significato: projectile: bullet, shot (heavy iron ball used for the shot put)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch coghele, either from or related to Middle High German kugele. If the word is inherited throughout Continental West Germanic, it requires a Proto-West Germanic *kugulā. From Middle Dutch croes, cruus, from Proto-West Germanic *krūs. Related with Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), whence Dutch krul. Further origin unknown. Possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس

parole.testo: From Middle Dutch lijstre (“thrush”), from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *lī(h)strō, of uncertain origin. From earlier nerve, from Middle Dutch *narwe, either inherited from Old Dutch *narwa or borrowed from Middle Low German narwe, eventually from Proto-Germanic *narwō, from earlier *arwaz (“scar”). For the change of -rwe → -rf, compare verf. Cognate with German Narbe (“scar”).

From Sranan Tongo nefo, neifo, from Dutch neef and/or from English nephew/neve, both ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *nefō, from Proto-Germanic *nefô, from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Doublet of neef.

From the adjective Middle Dutch nutte (“useful”), or from Middle Dutch nut (“yield”), from Old Dutch *nut, from Proto-Germanic *nutją, *nutjō (“profit, yield, utility”), from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to seize; grasp; use”).

From Middle Dutch ocsele, either from Old Dutch *uokusala or borrowed from Old Frisian axele, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō (“shoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *aḱs- (“armpit”). Cognate with English axle (“armpit”), German Achsel (“armpit”), Latin axilla (“armpit”), Latin axis (“axle”), Greek άξονας
From Middle Dutch olm, from Old Dutch (only attested in toponyms), from Old French olme, from Latin ulmus. Alternatively, inherited from Proto-Germanic *elmaz.
From Old Dutch *ungiwis, from Proto-Germanic *un- + *gawissaz, or alternatively from a reconstruction of *unwissaz.

parole.significato: a rope (often protected with wooden beads), chain or brace for fixing a spar to the mast
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *rak, from Old Dutch *rak, from Proto-West Germanic *rak, from Proto-Germanic *raką (“cord, chain”). Alternatively borrowed from Middle Low German rak (“parrel”), from Old Saxon *rak, from the same West Germanic source above.

parole.testo: From Middle Dutch reecs, raecs, raecse (“chain”), of obscure origin. Perhaps from Old Dutch *rakis, itself of uncertain origin and with no known cognates in Germanic. From Middle Dutch schra (“dry; poor, scanty”), either from Proto-Germanic *skrēla- or Proto-Germanic *skrēha-. Further origin uncertain. From Middle Dutch seneschal, seneschael, either via Old French seneschal or directly from Latin siniscalcus, from Proto-Germanic *siniz (“old”) + *skalkaz (“knight, servant”), with its final element being influenced by its cognate native Dutch schalk.
From Middle Dutch spelte, from Old Dutch *spelta, either from Frankish *spelta or Latin spelta, both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *spiltaz.

From Middle Dutch stap. Possibly from the same Germanic form from which English step derives (Proto-Germanic *stapiz) but with the vowel reverted to -a- by analogy with the verb stappen; alternatively from a closely related form that was not subject to i-umlaut.

From Middle Dutch sterven, from Old Dutch stervan, from Proto-Germanic *sterbaną, itself either from Proto-Indo-European *(s)terp- (“to lose force; lose sensibility, become numb; be dead, be motionless”) or from *sterbʰ- (“to be stiff, become stiff”).

From Middle Dutch tooch, from Old Dutch togen (“to show”), from Proto-West Germanic *taugijan or *ataugijan, from Proto-Germanic *at + *augijaną (“to display”), similar to Gothic 𐌰𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ataugjan, “to show”). Alternatively from Proto-Germanic *ta + *augijaną.

From Middle Dutch warm, from Old Dutch warm, from Proto-West Germanic *warm, from Proto-Germanic *warmaz, of uncertain origin; derivations from either Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”) or *wer- (“to burn”) have been proposed.
